sourceIssues.locator: §1.4.3, p. 13, lines 1–3 after Hypotheses 1.4.4, in arXiv v5; present in v4 at p. 12
sourceIssues.printed: "let Z ⊂ Z_G(A) be any closed subgroup such that Z_G(A)/Z is compact; for example, one can take Z to be the group of real points of the maximal F-split subgroup of Z_G"

sourceIssues.locator: §1.4.3, p. 13, formulas (4)–(6), in arXiv v5; present in v4 at pp. 12–13
sourceIssues.printed: "Assume moreover that we are given non-degenerate pairings of G(F_v)-spaces ⟨,⟩_{π_v}: π_v ⊗ π_v^∨ → C for all v. Then there is a constant C = C(dg, fac_π, fac_{π^∨}, ∏_v⟨,⟩_{π_v}) such that … ⟨φ, φ^∨⟩_Z = C(…) ∏_v ⟨φ_v, φ_v^∨⟩_{π_v}."
sourceIssues.correction: Add the hypothesis that for almost all v the local pairings satisfy ⟨φ_v^0, φ_v^{∨,0}⟩_{π_v} = 1 for the distinguished vectors used to form the restricted tensor products ⊗′π_v, ⊗′π_v^∨ (implicit in fac_π, fac_{π^∨}); only then is ∏_v ⟨φ_v, φ_v^∨⟩_{π_v} a finite product and (6) meaningful.
sourceIssues.reason: For factorizable φ = ⊗φ_v, φ_v = φ_v^0 for almost all v; with arbitrary non-degenerate local pairings the factors ⟨φ_v^0, φ_v^{∨,0}⟩ are arbitrary non-zero numbers and the infinite product need not converge. With the normalization, existence of C follows from Schur's lemma (Hom_{G(A)}(π ⊗ π^∨, C) is one-dimensional). Defence: the standard local pairing (7) with spherical vectors normalized by f(1) = 1 satisfies the normalization automatically (vol K_v = 1), and this is what the paper uses later.
searched: arXiv:1602.01776 v1 (February 2016), v2, v3 and v4 at the same place: Present in v1 (pp. 11–12) and v4 (pp. 12–13).

sourceIssues.locator: §1.4.3, p. 14, sentence after (7), in arXiv v5; present in v4 at p. 13
sourceIssues.printed: "In situation (2) of Hypotheses 1.4.4, we take K_v = ∏_i GL(n_i, O_i); however, the pairing (7) does not depend on the choice of K_v."
sourceIssues.correction: Replace 'however, the pairing (7) does not depend on the choice of K_v' by 'changing K_v to bK_vb^{-1} (b ∈ B) multiplies the pairing (7) by δ_B(b); we fix K_v as stated'.
sourceIssues.reason: Computation: ∫_{gK_vg^{−1}} F = ∫_{K_v} F(gkg^{−1})dk = ∫_{K_v} φ(gk)dk with φ = F(·g^{−1}); writing g = bk_0 this is δ_B(b)∫_{K_v} φ = δ_B(b)∫_{K_v} F by the G-invariance of ∫_{K_v}. Explicit case: G = GL_2(Q_p), B upper triangular, K = GL_2(Z_p), K′ = diag(p,1)K diag(p,1)^{−1} (hyperspecial, volume 1 for the same Haar measure), F(bk) = δ_B(b) the K-spherical vector with F(1) = 1. For k′ = (a, pb; c/p, d) ∈ K′, F(k′) = |det k′|/max(|c/p|,|d|)² equals 1 if p | c and p^{−2} if c ∈ Z_p^× (probability p/(p+1)), so ∫_{K′} F = 1/(p+1) + p^{−1}/(p+1) = p^{−1} = δ_B(diag(p,1)) ≠ 1 = ∫_K F. Defence: the discrepancy is a constant absorbed into C of (6), so nothing breaks if one K_v is used consistently. Independent check: The quote on p. 14 is accurate. It is also in v4 (p. 13, (1.4.5)) and absent from v3, where the sentence stops at 'we take K_v = ∏_i GL(n_i, O_i)'. For F(bx) = δ_B(b)F(x), the functional Λ_K(F) = ∫_K F dg is G-invariant. If K′ = gKg^{-1} with g = bk_0 (Iwasawa), then ∫_{K′}F dg = ∫_K F(gkg^{-1})dk = ∫_K φ(gk)dk with φ = R(g^{-1})F, which equals δ_B(b)Λ_K(φ) = δ_B(b)Λ_K(F). Here vol(K′) = vol(K) because G is unimodular. I checked the first reading's GL_2(Q_p) example directly. Take K′ = diag(p,1)GL_2(Z_p)diag(p,1)^{-1} and let F be the K-spherical δ_B-function with F(1) = 1 (this is f·f^∨ for the normalised spherical vectors). Then F(k′) = 1 when p | c and p^{-2} when c is a unit; the second case has proportion p/(p+1). So ∫_{K′}F = 1/p ≠ 1 = ∫_K F. The pairing (7) therefore depends on K_v through the positive scalar δ_B(b). The claim is false as stated. It is harmless because the scalar is absorbed into C of (6) once K_v is fixed, which the paper does.
searched: arXiv:1602.01776 v1 (February 2016), v2, v3 and v4 at the same place: The sentence was added in v4 (p. 13, equation (1.4.5)); v1–v3 define the pairing without the independence claim.

sourceIssues.locator: §2.1, p. 15, last lines (equivalence of quadruples), in arXiv v5; present in v4 at p. 14
sourceIssues.printed: "two quadruples (A, λ, ι, α) and (A′, λ′, ι′, α′) are equivalent if there exists a prime-to-□ isogeny f : A → A′ such that λ equals f^∨∘λ′∘f up to some positive element in Z_(□)^×, ι′(b)∘f = f∘ι(b) for all b ∈ O_B, and α′ = f∘α."
sourceIssues.correction: "prime-to-□ quasi-isogeny" (a Z_(□)^×-isogeny as in Lan's isogeny-class formulation), or 'the equivalence relation generated by' the printed relation.
sourceIssues.reason: With genuine isogenies the relation is not symmetric: for □ = {p}, if f has degree prime to p and g: A′ → A satisfies g∘f = [N] (N prime to p), then g∘α′ = g∘f∘α = N·α, which is not in the K^□-orbit of α in general (N·1 ∉ K^□ when K^□ ⊂ G(Ẑ^p)). Defence: 'isogeny' for 'quasi-isogeny' is a common abuse and the reference to Lan's representability theorem fixes the meaning.
searched: arXiv:1602.01776 v1 (February 2016), v2, v3 and v4 at the same place: Present in v1 (p. 12) and v4 (p. 14).

sourceIssues.locator: §2.2, p. 16, definition of the signature of h, in arXiv v5; present in v4 at p. 15
sourceIssues.printed: "The homomorphism h determines a pure Hodge structure of weight −1 on V = L ⊗ C. Let V^0 ⊂ V be the degree 0 piece of the Hodge filtration; this is an O_B ⊗ C-submodule. For each σ ∈ Σ_𝒦, let a_{σ,i} = dim_C e_i(V^0 ⊗_{O⊗C,σ} C)."
sourceIssues.correction: V^0 should be V^{−1,0} ≅ V/V^{0,−1} (the summand on which h(z) acts by z; Lan's V_0, the Lie-algebra side of the Kottwitz determinant condition), not the degree-0 Hodge filtration step F^0V = V^{0,−1}.
sourceIssues.reason: Convention-free check against §2.6.1/§2.6.3 (p. 21–22): there W = V/V^{0,−1}, Λ_0 ⊗ C = W, and 'e_iΛ_{0,σ} and e_iΛ^∨_{0,σ} are free S′_0-modules of respective ranks a_{σ,i} and b_{σ,i}'. But dim e_i(V/V^{0,−1})_σ = n_i − dim e_i(F^0V)_σ, which with the printed definition is b_{σ,i}, not a_{σ,i} (the weight −1 Hodge filtration is F^{−1} = V ⊃ F^0 = V^{0,−1} ⊃ F^1 = 0). Second check (Deligne's sign convention, h(z) acts on V^{p,q} by z^{−p}z̄^{−q}, the one compatible with weight −1 for an R-algebra homomorphism h): in §2.3, for σ ∈ Σ, h(z) acts on the σ-component V_{i,σ} by diag(z 1_{r_{i,σ}}, z̄ 1_{s_{i,σ}}), so F^0 = V^{0,−1} (h(z) = z̄) has dimension s_{i,σ}, contradicting '(a_{σ,i}, b_{σ,i}) equals (r_{i,σ}, s_{i,σ}) if σ ∈ Σ'. With V^0 = V^{−1,0} both statements hold. Likely origin: Lan's notation V_0 (subscript) for the h(z) = z part read as a Hodge degree. Defence: the symmetry (a_{σc}, b_{σc}) = (b_σ, a_σ), the reflex field formula and all later uses are consistent with the corrected reading.
searched: arXiv:1602.01776 v1 (February 2016), v2, v3 and v4 at the same place: Present in v1 (p. 13), v2/v3 (p. 14), v4 (p. 15); §2.6.3 rank statement likewise unchanged since v1.

sourceIssues.locator: §2.3, p. 17, construction of P from hermitian pairs, in arXiv v5; present in v4 at pp. 15–16
sourceIssues.printed: "Let δ ∈ O be totally imaginary and prime to p, and put ⟨·,·⟩_i = trace_{𝒦/Q} δ⟨·,·⟩_{V_i}. … let h_{i,σ} : C → End_R(V_{i,σ}) be h_{i,σ}(z) = diag(z1_{r_{i,σ}}, z̄1_{s_{i,σ}}). Let Σ = {σ ∈ Σ_𝒦 : p_σ ∈ Σ_p}. … Then P = (B, ∗, O_B, L, 2π√−1⟨·,·⟩, h) is a PEL datum of unitary type"
sourceIssues.correction: δ must also satisfy a sign condition tied to the CM type Σ: Im σ(δ) > 0 for all σ ∈ Σ if ⟨·,·⟩_{V_i} is 𝒦-linear in the first variable (Im σ(δ) < 0 for all σ ∈ Σ if linear in the second). Such δ exist (weak approximation), so the fix is to choose δ after Σ.
sourceIssues.reason: Positivity axiom of a PEL datum: −√−1 · 2π√−1⟨x, h(√−1)x⟩ = 2π Σ_{σ∈Σ} 2Re(σ(δ) H_σ(x_σ, h(i)x_σ)). With H linear in the first variable: on the r-part (H_σ(x,x) = |x|² > 0, h(i)x = ix) the summand is 2|x|² Im σ(δ); on the s-part (H_σ(x,x) = −|x|², h(i)x = −ix) it is again 2|x|² Im σ(δ). So the form is positive definite iff Im σ(δ) > 0 for every σ ∈ Σ with V_{i,σ} ≠ 0. Σ is determined by the p-adic datum Σ_p and δ only by 'totally imaginary and prime to p', so for a general δ the positivity fails on some V_{i,σ}. The text never states such a condition later (δ reappears in §4.1 only as ⟨·,·⟩_1 = trace δ⟨·,·⟩_V). Defence: the requirement is implicit in the claim that P is a PEL datum and is trivially arranged; alternatively one could flip h_{i,σ} at the offending σ, but that would change the stated relation between (a, b) and (r, s). Independent check: The quote on p. 17 is accurate. δ is only required to be totally imaginary and prime to p, and it is chosen before Σ = {σ : p_σ ∈ Σ_p} is defined. The positivity axiom (p. 14) for the pairing 2π√−1⟨·,·⟩ reads 2π⟨x, h(√−1)x⟩ > 0. On V_i ⊗ R = ⊕_{σ∈Σ} V_{i,σ} we have ⟨x, h(i)x⟩_i = Σ_{σ∈Σ} 2Re(σ(δ)H_σ(x_σ, h_{i,σ}(i)x_σ)). Take H linear in the first variable. On the r-part, h(i)x = ix and H(x,x) = |x|². On the s-part, h(i)x = −ix and H(x,x) = −|x|². In both cases the summand is 2 Im σ(δ)|x|². So positivity holds iff Im σ(δ) > 0 for every σ ∈ Σ with V_{i,σ} ≠ 0 (the reverse sign if H is linear in the second variable). The compatibility ⟨h(z)x, y⟩ = ⟨x, h(z̄)y⟩ holds for every δ, but positivity does not. Replacing δ by −δ, which is allowed, destroys it. Flipping h at the offending σ would contradict the stated equality (a_{σ,i}, b_{σ,i}) = (r_{i,σ}, s_{i,σ}) for σ ∈ Σ. So 'P is a PEL datum' can fail for admissible δ. The fix is trivial: choose δ after Σ with the right signs. Present in v1 (p. 14) and v4 (pp. 15–16).

sourceIssues.locator: §2.3.2, p. 18, lines 6–8 of §2.3.2, in arXiv v5; present in v4 at pp. 16–17
sourceIssues.printed: "Suppose 𝒦_1, …, 𝒦_r are finite CM extensions of 𝒦 with Σ_{i=1}^r [𝒦_i : 𝒦] = n. … Let V′_i = 𝒦_i, viewed as a 𝒦-space of dimension [𝒦_i : 𝒦]. Each V′_i can be given a 𝒦_i-hermitian structure such that ⊕_i V′_i is isomorphic to V as an hermitian space over 𝒦."
sourceIssues.correction: This must be a hypothesis on (𝒦_1, …, 𝒦_r) ('Suppose each V′_i can be given …'); it holds e.g. when all 𝒦_i = 𝒦, but not for arbitrary CM extensions.
sourceIssues.reason: Counterexample: 𝒦 = Q(i), p ≡ 1 mod 4, n = 2, r = 1, 𝒦_1 = Q(i, √2) (CM, 𝒦_1⁺ = Q(√2)), V = 𝒦² with ⟨x, y⟩_V = x_1ȳ_1 + 3x_2ȳ_2 (definite, admissible in §2.3). The 𝒦-hermitian forms on 𝒦_1 for which 𝒦_1 acts by ⟨ax, y⟩ = ⟨x, āy⟩ are Tr_{𝒦_1/𝒦}(αxȳ), α ∈ Q(√2)^×; in the 𝒦-basis {1, √2} their Gram matrix is [[2a_0, 4a_1],[4a_1, 4a_0]] (α = a_0 + a_1√2), of determinant 8N(α). Hence ⊕V′_i ≅ V would force 3 · 8N(α) ∈ N_{𝒦/Q}(𝒦^×). At the place 3 (inert in Q(i) and in Q(√2)), norms from Q_3(i) and from Q_3(√2) have even 3-adic valuation, while 24N(α) has odd valuation: impossible. Equivalently, 𝒦_1 ⊗_{Q} Q_3 splits over 𝒦 ⊗ Q_3 with the involution swapping the factors, so every such trace form is hyperbolic at 3, whereas V ⊗ Q_3 is anisotropic (−3 is not a norm from Q_3(i)). Defence: the only case used for the standing assumption is 𝒦_i = 𝒦 (always possible by diagonalization), and §3.2.4 only uses CM pairs (J_0′, h_0) that exist. Independent check: The quote on p. 18 is accurate. It is stated as a fact for arbitrary CM extensions K_i/K. I verified the counterexample. The K-hermitian forms on K_1 = Q(i, √2) = Q(ζ_8) (with K_1^+ = Q(√2)) compatible with the K_1-action are Tr_{K_1/K}(αxȳ), α = a_0 + a_1√2 ∈ Q(√2)^×. In the basis {1, √2} the Gram matrix is [[2a_0, 4a_1],[4a_1, 4a_0]], of determinant 8N(α). An isometry with V = ⟨1, 3⟩ over Q(i) needs 24N(α) ∈ N(Q(i)^×). But 3 is inert in both Q(i) and Q(√2), so v_3(24N(α)) is odd while local norms from Q_3(i) have even valuation. Equivalently, K_1 ⊗_K K_3 ≅ Q_9 × Q_9 with the involution swapping the factors, so every such form is hyperbolic at 3, whereas V ⊗ Q_3 is anisotropic. V (with δ = i, lattice O², p ≡ 1 mod 4, p ≠ 3) satisfies the §2.3 set-up. The sentence must be a hypothesis on (K_i). The only case the paper needs is K_i = K, where it holds by diagonalisation. Present in v1 (p. 15) and v4 (p. 17).

sourceIssues.locator: §2.3, p. 18, lines 3–5, in arXiv v5; present in v4 at p. 16
sourceIssues.printed: "More precisely, the elements of ker¹(Q, G) classify isomorphism classes of hermitian tuples 𝒱′ = (V′_j, ⟨·,·⟩_{V′_j})_{1≤j≤m} that are locally isomorphic to 𝒱 at every place of Q."
sourceIssues.correction: They classify tuples that are locally similar to 𝒱 at every place (V′_j ⊗ Q_v ≅ c_v·(V_j ⊗ Q_v) with a common c_v ∈ Q_v^× for all j), up to global similitude with a common factor c ∈ Q^×.
sourceIssues.reason: G is a similitude group, so H¹(Q, G) and H¹(Q_v, G) classify hermitian tuples up to similitude, not up to isometry. Read literally, the printed sentence makes ker¹(Q, G) trivial: by Landherr's theorem (Hasse principle for hermitian forms over a CM extension), hermitian spaces that are isomorphic at every place are globally isomorphic, so there would be a single class — contradicting the next paragraph, which says the Hasse principle fails in general when dim V_1 is odd. Defence: the intended statement is Kottwitz's [Kot92, §7–§8], which the paper cites. Independent check: The quote on p. 18 is accurate. G = G_P is the similitude group with a common factor ν. From 1 → U → G → G_m → 1 and H¹(Q, G_m) = 1 we get H¹(Q,G) = H¹(Q,U)/Q^×, and likewise locally. So ker¹(Q,G) classifies tuples that are locally similar everywhere, with a common c_v at each v, modulo a common global similitude. With the standard meaning of 'isomorphic' (isometric), tuples locally isometric to 𝒱 everywhere are globally isometric by Landherr's Hasse principle for hermitian forms over K/K^+. The set would then be a singleton, which contradicts the next paragraph: ker¹ ≠ 0 in general when dim V_1 is odd or m > 1. The paper never says that isomorphisms are similitudes. The intended statement is Kottwitz's, and nothing downstream is affected. Present in v1 (p. 14) and v4 (p. 16).

sourceIssues.locator: §2.5, p. 20, last lines before (14), in arXiv v5; present in v4 at pp. 18–19
sourceIssues.printed: "and M̄_{K_r/F} (resp. M̄_{K_r,L/F}) is the normalization of M^tor_{K/F} (resp. M^tor_{K,L/F}) in M_{K_r/F} (resp. M_{K_r,L}/F)."
sourceIssues.correction: M̄_{K_r/F} is an open subscheme of that normalization (dense, containing M_{K_r/F}), in general a proper one: the normalization is finite over M^tor_{K/F}, whereas M̄_{K_r/F} is not.
sourceIssues.reason: The normalization of M^tor_{K/F} in M_{K_r/F} is finite over M^tor_{K/F}. The paper itself says M̄_{K_r} is étale and quasi-finite but not finite over M^tor_K, and this already holds in characteristic 0: over a boundary point, 𝒜^∨ has a non-trivial torus part and 𝒜^∨[p^r] has fewer geometric points than over M_K, so there are fewer injections L⁺ ⊗ μ_{p^r} ↪ 𝒜^∨[p^r]. Since M̄_{K_r/F} is normal (étale over a smooth scheme) and quasi-finite over M^tor_{K/F}, Zariski's main theorem makes it an open subscheme of the normalization, missing the boundary points where the level structure does not extend. Modular-curve case: over X(1) with the Tate curve at ∞, μ_p ↪ E[p] has p² − 1 geometric choices generically but only p − 1 over the cusp (those onto the canonical μ_p); the normalization X_μ(p) has in addition the (p − 1) cusps ramified of index p, which are not in M̄. Defence: later sections use M̄_{K_r} as defined (sections of ω_{r,κ} over M̄_{K_r}, §2.6.6), not the normalization, and the Koecher principle (20) compares with sections over M_{K_r}; the claim is not used in an essential way, though the definition of cusp forms S_κ(K_r, ψ; R) via D_{∞,r} = M̄_{K_r} − M_{K_r} only imposes vanishing at the boundary present in M̄_{K_r}. Independent check: The quote on p. 20 is accurate; the printed text has 'M_{K_r,L/F}'. The same paragraph says that M̄_{K_r} (resp. M̄_{K_r,L}) is étale and quasi-finite but not finite over M^tor_K. A normalization of the excellent scheme M^tor_{K/F} in M_{K_r/F} is finite over it. So the two statements are incompatible unless M̄_{K_r/F} is finite. It is not finite, even over F. At a boundary point, 𝒜^∨ has a torus part, so 𝒜^∨[p^r] has fewer geometric points. Injections L^+⊗μ_{p^r} ↪ 𝒜^∨[p^r] that do not land in the toric part do not specialise. In the modular-curve analogue, μ_p ↪ E[p] over the Tate curve has p² − 1 generic choices but only p − 1 at the cusp, and the normalization has p − 1 further cusps with ramification index p. M̄_{K_r/F} is normal, quasi-finite and separated over M^tor_{K/F}, and it contains M_{K_r/F} densely (étale maps are open). By Zariski's main theorem it is a dense open subscheme of the normalization, in general a proper one. The paper works with M̄_{K_r} as defined, so the sentence itself carries no weight. A caveat not decided here: the cusp forms S_κ(K_r,ψ;R) = H⁰(M̄_{K_r}, ω(−D_{∞,r})) only require vanishing at the boundary strata present in M̄_{K_r}. §2.6.7's identification of them with classical cusp forms of level K_r therefore cannot rest on this sentence.

sourceIssues.correction: The identification induced by a basis of Z_p(1) (i.e. μ_{p^r} ≅ Z/p^r) is defined over F(μ_{p^r}) (in particular on C-points), not over F. Over F, M_{K_r/F} corresponds to the level group I_r′ ⊂ I_r^0 that acts on L⁻ unipotently and on L⁺ with diagonal ν, rather than to I_r.
sourceIssues.reason: For (A, α) ∈ M_{I_rK^p}, π_1-stability of the I_r-orbit of α_t: L ⊗ Z/p^r ≅ A_t[p^r] means σ∘α_t = α_t∘g_σ with g_σ ∈ I_r, and I_r acts unipotently on L⁺; so α_t(L⁺/p^r) is a subgroup with trivial Galois action on its graded pieces (constant type), while L⁻ carries the cyclotomic character through ν. For M_{K_r}, φ(L⁺ ⊗ μ_{p^r}) is a μ-type subgroup. These moduli problems agree after trivializing μ_{p^r}, which requires μ_{p^r} ⊂ base; μ_p ⊄ F for p odd since p is unramified in F ⊂ 𝒦′. (Compare Y_μ(N) and Y_1(N) over Q.) Defence: all later uses compare classical forms with automorphic forms over C (or over rings containing μ_{p^∞}), where the identification is valid; v1–v3 wrote 'a basis of Z(1)', suggesting the analytic identification over C was meant.

sourceIssues.reason: Counterexample: in one GL_{n_i}(O_w)-factor take j ≤ a_{w,i}, j < n_i, and g = 1 + p^r E_{j+1,1} ∈ I_r^0 (the (j+1,1) entry lies in the strictly lower part of the A-block or in the C-block, both ≡ 0 mod p^r for elements of I_r^0; the other components of g are 1 and ν = 1, allowed by (9)). Then t^+ g (t^+)^{−1} = 1 + p^{r−1}E_{j+1,1}, which is not in B^+ mod p^r. Similarly for a_{w,i} < j < n_i with g = 1 + p^rE_{a+1,1}. Conjugation by t^+ divides the entries (k,l) with t_k/t_l = p^{−1} by p, and these are lower-left entries. The inclusion holds only for j = n_i (t^+ central in that factor). Defence: the intended meaning (t^+ is 'positive', contracting N^+ and expanding N^−) is standard and is what the definition of U_{w,i,j} needs; the inclusion is not used in any proof. Independent check: The quote on p. 26 is accurate. I_r^0 = {g ∈ G(Z_p) : g mod p^r ∈ B^+(Z/p^r)} with B^+ as in (14): A upper-triangular, D lower-triangular, C ≡ 0. Conjugation by t = t^+_{w,i,j} multiplies the (k,l) entry by t_k/t_l. Take j ≤ a, j < n_i, and g = 1 + p^rE_{j+1,1} ∈ I_r^0 in one GL_{n_i}(O_w) factor. Then tgt^{-1} = 1 + p^{r−1}E_{j+1,1}. Its (j+1,1) entry lies in the strictly lower part of A or in C, where elements of I_r^0 must be ≡ 0 mod p^r. So tgt^{-1} ∉ I_r^0. The case a < j < n_i is analogous (entry (a+1,1), or an upper entry of D when a = 0). The reverse inclusion t^{-1}I_r^0t ⊂ I_r^0 also fails: it divides free upper entries by p. What holds is the standard positivity, which is what the definition of U_{w,i,j} (23) needs: t contracts N^+(Z_p) and t^{-1} contracts N^−(p^rZ_p). The printed inclusion is used nowhere. sourceIssues.locator: §2.9.4, p. 32, lines 5–8, arXiv v5
sourceIssues.printed: Fixing G_m = Spec(Z[x, 1/x]) ... yields ... an identification Lie_{Z_p}(μ_{p^n}) = Z x d/dx. For any scheme S, this identifies Lie_S(μ_{p^n}) with O_S, compatibly as n varies.

sourceIssues.locator: §2.9.4, p. 32, justification of injectivity of (28), arXiv v5
sourceIssues.printed: – these are injective because, as already noted, S_1 is dense in the special fiber of M^tor_{K,L} –
sourceIssues.correction: Injectivity of M_κ(K_r, ψ; R) → V_{κ_p}(K^p, ψ, R) needs (for R flat over Z_p): every connected component of \overline{M}_{K_r,L/R} meets the special fibre, plus p-adic separatedness of H^0. Density of the ordinary locus in the special fibre of M^tor_{K,L} gives this at level K, not directly at level K_r.
sourceIssues.reason: The special fibre of \overline{M}_{K_r} already lies over the ordinary locus (a closed immersion L^+ ⊗ μ_{p^r} ↪ A^∨[p^r] in characteristic p forces ordinarity under Hypothesis 2.2.1), and \overline{M}_{K_r} is only quasi-finite over M^tor_K, so the density of S_1 in the special fibre of M^tor_{K,L} does not by itself rule out components of the generic fibre of \overline{M}_{K_r,L} whose closure misses the special fibre (sections supported there would have f_{p-adic} = 0). Defence: the needed fact is standard in Hida's theory (e.g. via the q-expansion principle or irreducibility of Igusa towers, [Hid04, Ch. 8], [Lan18]), and the statement is true; only the justification is too brief.
searched: arXiv:1602.01776 v1 (February 2016), v2, v3 and v4 at the same place: Same in v4 (p. 29).

sourceIssues.printed: Let R be as in Equation (32) and let O^+ denote the integral closure of Z_(p) in R. The fraction field Frac(O^+) of O^+ is a number field over which S_κ(K_r, ψ; R) ⊗ Q has a rational model
sourceIssues.correction: Let O^+ be the localisation at the prime above p (determined by incl_p) of the ring of integers of a number field E_0 ⊂ Frac(R) over which S_κ(K_r, ψ; ·) has a rational model (e.g. E_0 containing K′ and the values of ψ); equivalently, the integral closure of Z_(p) in E_0.
sourceIssues.reason: R is a finite O′[ψ]-domain, e.g. R = Z_p or O′. The integral closure of Z_(p) in Z_p is Z_p ∩ \overline{Q}, whose fraction field Q_p ∩ \overline{Q} has infinite degree over Q (it contains √(1 + p^2 k) for all integers k, p odd, hence infinitely many quadratic fields). So Frac(O^+) is never a number field. Defence: any sufficiently large number field works for the definition of 'ordinary complex cusp forms relative to ι' that follows, and O^+ is not used elsewhere in the paper. Independent check: The quote on pp. 33–34 is accurate. R is a finite O′- or O′[ψ]-domain, where O′ is the ring of integers of the finite extension L′ of Q_p (p. 30). So R ⊃ Z_p. The integral closure of Z_(p) in R contains Z_p ∩ Q̄. For odd p, √(1 + p²k) ∈ Z_p for every integer k, and these generate infinitely many quadratic fields. So Frac(O^+) ⊇ Q_p ∩ Q̄ has infinite degree over Q and is never a number field. The intended object is the p-integers of a suitable number field E_0 carrying the rational model. O^+ is used only in this paragraph, to define 'ordinary complex cusp forms relative to ι'. Present in v1–v4 (v4 p. 30).

Independent check: The quote on p. 35 is accurate. For p = 2, K = Q(√−7) satisfies them (2 splits, K^+ = Q). Then O_w = Z_2, the torsion of O_w^× is {±1} while k_w^× = 1, so the displayed Δ ≅ ∏(k_w^×)^{a_{w,i}} fails. sourceIssues.locator: Proposition 3.2.5(ii), proof, p. 41, arXiv v5
sourceIssues.printed: Note that V^ord_{κ_p}((G, X); K^p, R) is the R-dual to a finite rank module over an appropriate Iwasawa algebra, by Hida theory; thus f belongs to a finite rank R module. Point (ii) follows from the Zariski density of the ordinary locus in the integral model of S(G, X) [Wed99], provided we know there are enough CM points in the ordinary locus. But every point on the ordinary locus over a finite field lifts ... to the generic fiber (see for example [Moo04, Proposition 2.3.12]).
sourceIssues.correction: A complete argument: every F̄_p-point of the ordinary locus is the reduction of an ordinary CM point (Serre–Tate canonical lift) and the Igusa tower over it is covered by the Igusa towers (46) of CM pairs and their prime-to-p Hecke translates; hence f mod p vanishes at all F̄_p-points of the reduced Igusa varieties T_{n,1}, so f ≡ 0 mod p; since T_{n,m} is flat over Z/p^m and the value of p·g at a canonical lift depends only on g mod p, induction on m gives f ≡ 0 mod p^m for all m (for R flat over Z_p; general R by the same dévissage), so f = 0.
sourceIssues.reason: The printed proof invokes the density of the ordinary locus in the integral model, which is irrelevant for a p-adic form (a function on the formal Igusa tower over the ordinary locus), and never explains how vanishing at the (discrete) set of CM points forces a function on a formal scheme to vanish; the finite-rank remark is not used. Also the Igusa tower of S(J′_0, h_0) must meet every point of each fibre of the Igusa tower, which needs the CM pairs to be taken with all their Hecke translates. Defence: the conclusion is true and the ingredients cited (canonical lifts) suffice once the p-adic dévissage is added; ordinarity of f is not needed for this route.

sourceIssues.locator: §4.1.4, p. 45, lines 5–12 (the paragraph after the definition of I(φ, φ^♭, f, s)), in arXiv v5
sourceIssues.printed: “Moreover, it follows from the unfolding in [GPSR87] that, for any pair π, π′ of automorphic representations of G_1, the map (φ, φ′) ↦ I(φ, φ′, f, s) defines a G_1(𝔸)-invariant pairing between π and π′. The multiplicity one hypothesis 7.3.3 implies that the space of such pairings is at most one-dimensional, and is exactly one-dimensional provided π′ = π^∨ (upon restriction to U(V). Thus: If ⟨φ, φ^♭⟩ = 0 then I(φ, φ^♭, f, s) = 0 for all s.”
sourceIssues.correction: For fixed f the map (φ, φ′) ↦ I(φ, φ′, f, s) is not G_1(𝔸)-invariant. Only the trilinear form in (f, φ, φ′) is invariant, and f transforms by the diagonal translation. What is true, using Hypothesis 7.3.3: after unfolding, I depends on (φ, φ′) only through the L² pairings ⟨π(u)φ, φ′⟩, so I ≡ 0 unless π′ ≅ π^∨ (on U(V)). The implication ‘⟨φ, φ^♭⟩ = 0 ⇒ I(φ, φ^♭, f, s) = 0’ is false in general.
sourceIssues.reason: By the unfolding (p. 45), I(π(h)φ, π′(h)φ′, f, s) = ∫ f((huh^{-1}, 1))⟨π(u)φ, φ′⟩ du, which differs from I(φ, φ′, f, s) unless f((huh^{-1},1)) = f((u,1)). Concretely, I = c·∏_v Z_v, where Z_v(φ_v, φ^♭_v, f_v) = ⟨π_v(F_v)φ_v, φ^♭_v⟩ with F_v(u) = f_v((u,1)). Take v ∈ S_π (or v = ∞), where the statement allows arbitrary f_v and φ_v. Sections supported in the open cell P_v(U_{1,v} × 1) give arbitrary F_v ∈ C_c^∞(U_{1,v}), for instance F_v = char(g_0K′). Then one can choose φ_v, φ^♭_v with ⟨φ_v, φ^♭_v⟩ = 0 but ⟨π_v(F_v)φ_v, φ^♭_v⟩ ≠ 0, which gives ⟨φ, φ^♭⟩ = 0 while I ≠ 0 for Re(s) ≫ 0. Uniqueness of invariant pairings π × π′ → ℂ comes from Schur's lemma, not from multiplicity one. Hypothesis 7.3.3 (π′ occurs with multiplicity one in the cuspidal spectrum) is what makes the L² pairing between π and π′ vanish unless π′ is the realisation of π^∨. Defence: the paper immediately assumes ⟨φ, φ^♭⟩ ≠ 0 and uses only (51), which is correct under that assumption. For the specific ramified sections of §4.2.2 one does have Z_v = vol(𝒰_v)⟨φ_v, φ^♭_v⟩. Independent check: The quote on p. 45 is accurate. Replace φ, φ′ by π(h)φ, π′(h)φ′ and change variables (g_1,g_2) ↦ (g_1,g_2)(h,h)^{-1}. This moves (h,h) onto f by right translation, and f is not right-invariant. Equivalently, after unfolding, I(π(h)φ, π(h)φ^♭) = ∫ f((huh^{-1},1))⟨π(u)φ,φ^♭⟩du. Here (h,h) ∈ P, since it stabilises V^d, so f((huh^{-1},1)) = χ(det h)f((u,1)(h,h)^{-1}), which is not f((u,1)) in general. So for fixed f the map is not G_1(A)-invariant. For factorizable data, I = c∏_v⟨π_v(F_v)φ_v, φ^♭_v⟩ with F_v(u) = f_v((u,1)). u ↦ P(u,1) is an open embedding (the paper cites [HLS06] for openness; injectivity holds because (u,1) ∈ P forces u = 1). So at v ∈ S_π or at ∞, F_v can be any function in C_c^∞. Wherever π_v has dimension > 1, one can take ⟨φ_v,φ^♭_v⟩ = 0 and ⟨π_v(F_v)φ_v,φ^♭_v⟩ ≠ 0. That gives ⟨φ,φ^♭⟩ = 0 but I ≠ 0 for Re s ≫ 0, so the displayed implication is false. Uniqueness of invariant pairings on irreducible π × π′ is Schur's lemma, not Hypothesis 7.3.3. The paper then assumes ⟨φ,φ^♭⟩ ≠ 0, and (51), Theorem 4.6.1 and the rest do not use the implication. Same argument in v4 (p. 40); absent in v1.

sourceIssues.locator: §4.2.1, pp. 46–47, the displayed identity “d_{n,v}(s, χ_v) I_v(φ_v, φ′_v, f_v, s) = L_v(s + 1/2, π_v, χ_v)” with (53), in arXiv v5
sourceIssues.printed: “In either case, we have d_{n,v}(s, χ_v) I_v(φ_v, φ′_v, f_v, s) = L_v(s + 1/2, π_v, χ_v), where d_{n,v}(s, χ_v) = d_{n,v}(s) = ∏_{r=0}^{n−1} L_v(2s + n − r, χ_v|_{𝒦^+} η_v^r)” and “L_v(s, π_v, χ_v) = L_v(s, BC(π_v) ⊗ χ_v∘det)”
sourceIssues.correction: d_{n,v}(s, χ_v^{-1}) I_v(φ_v, φ′_v, f_v, s) = L_v(s+½, π_v, χ_v^{-1}), with L_v(s, π_v, χ) = L_v(s, BC(π_v) ⊗ χ∘det). Alternatively, keep the printed identity and replace χ by χ^{-1} in the definition of I(χ,s) (inducing from χ^{-1}(det∘Δ(·))δ_P^{-s/n}|ν|^{sn/2}, with the paper's δ_P = |det∘Δ|^n). The first reading's alternative 'χ^{-1}(det∘Δ)δ_P^{s/n}' is right only if δ_P means the true modulus character |det∘Δ|^{-n}. With the paper's δ_P it also flips s ↦ −s.
sourceIssues.reason: Right versus left action. Under the right action p acts on V^d by v ↦ vp, the inverse of the left action g·v := vg^{-1}. So χ(det Δ(p))|det Δ(p)|^{-s} = χ^{-1}(det Δ_left(p))|det Δ_left(p)|^{s}, and the paper's I(χ, s) is the left-action induced representation for χ^{-1} used in [GPSR87], [Li92], [HKS96]; the cited computations then give L(s+½, π, χ^{-1})/d(s, χ^{-1}). Direct check for n = 1 at a split unramified v: U(1)(𝒦_v^+) ≅ 𝒦_w^× via the action on V_w, and π_v = β. In (V_d, V^d)-coordinates (u, 1) = ((u+1)/2, (u−1)/2; (u−1)/2, (u+1)/2). The spherical section of Ind(ψ_{w,s}) takes value χ_w(d)χ_{w̄}^{-1}(a)|a/d|^{s+1/2} at a matrix with bottom row (γ, δ), where |d| = max(|γ|, |δ|) and ad = det. Hence f((u,1)) = χ_{w̄}^{-1}(u)|u|^{s+1/2} for |u| ≤ 1 and χ_w(u)|u|^{-s-1/2} for |u| ≥ 1, and ∫ f((u,1))β(u) d^×u = L(s+½, βχ_{w̄}^{-1}) L(s+½, β^{-1}χ_w^{-1}) / L(2s+1, (χ_wχ_{w̄})^{-1}). Equivalently, with Φ = char M_{1×2}(O_w) in (55), f^Φ(1) = L(2s+1, (χ_wχ_{w̄})^{-1}), and the substitution z_1 = xu, z_2 = x factors ∫ f^Φ((u,1))β(u) d^×u into these two Tate integrals. The printed formula predicts L(s+½, β^{±1}χ_w)L(s+½, β^{∓1}χ_{w̄}) / L(2s+1, χ_wχ_{w̄}), which is different for generic unramified χ_v. The corrected characters are exactly those in the p-adic factor of Theorem 4.3.10, L(s+½, π_b ⊗ χ_{2,w}) = L(s+½, π_b ⊗ χ_{w̄}^{-1}) and L(s+½, π̃_a ⊗ χ_{1,w}^{-1}) = L(s+½, π̃_a ⊗ χ_w^{-1}), so the p-adic computation agrees with the corrected unramified formula and the printed one is the odd one out. Defence: the identity is quoted from sources that use left actions, and the discrepancy is the relabelling χ ↦ χ^{-1} (complex conjugation for unitary χ), under which the construction is unchanged in substance. Independent check: The quotes on pp. 46–47 are accurate. I checked independently at n = 1, v = ww̄ split and unramified. I(χ,s) (§4.1.2) with Δ(p) = the V^d-block D restricts on the w-component to Ind(ψ_{w,s}): the w̄-part of Δ(p) is ᵗA^{-1}, so ψ_{w,s} = χ_w(D)χ_{w̄}^{-1}(A)|A/D|^s, and the normalised f(pg) = ψ δ^{1/2}f(g) with δ^{1/2} = |A/D|^{1/2}. This agrees with (55). In polarization coordinates (§4.1.1: (a,b) ↦ (a+b, b−a)), (u,1) = ½[[u+1, u−1],[u−1, u+1]]. So the spherical f with f(1) = 1 gives f((u,1)) = χ_{w̄}^{-1}(u)|u|^{s+1/2} for |u| ≤ 1 and χ_w(u)|u|^{-s-1/2} for |u| ≥ 1. With π_v = β, (51) gives I_v = Σ_{k≥0}X^k + Σ_{k≥1}Y^k, where X = χ_{w̄}^{-1}β(ϖ)q^{-s-1/2} and Y = (χ_wβ)^{-1}(ϖ)q^{-s-1/2}. This sums to (1−XY)/((1−X)(1−Y)) = L(s+½, βχ_{w̄}^{-1})L(s+½, β^{-1}χ_w^{-1})/L(2s+1, (χ_wχ_{w̄})^{-1}). The printed formula predicts denominator d_{1,v}(s,χ_v) = L(2s+1, χ_wχ_{w̄}) and numerator L(s+½, β^{±1}χ_w)L(s+½, β^{∓1}χ_{w̄}). These agree with the computation only when χ_wχ_{w̄}(ϖ) = 1, i.e. χ|_{K^+} is trivial at v, whatever identification of U(1) or BC is used. So the identity holds with χ_v^{-1}. The cause is the right action: the paper's I(χ,s) is the left-action I(s, χ^{-1}) of [Li92]/[GPSR87]. The p-adic factors of Theorem 4.3.10 (L(s+½, π_b ⊗ χ_{w̄}^{-1}), L(s+½, π̃_a ⊗ χ_w^{-1})) match the corrected form. This propagates to the statement of Theorem 4.6.1 (D(χ), L^S(s+½, π, χ_u)), up to the relabelling χ ↦ χ^{-1} = χ̄. Identical in v4 (p. 41) and v1 (p. 39).

sourceIssues.locator: Lemma 4.2.3 and its proof, §4.2.2, p. 48, first display of the proof (“for g ∈ U_{1,v} × 1_n, f^-_{L_v}(g) = δ_{−1_n·𝒰_v×1_n}(g)”), in arXiv v5
sourceIssues.printed: “The support of f^-_{L_v} in U_{1,v} × 1_n is −1_n·𝒰_v × 1_n, and for g ∈ U_{1,v} × 1_n, f^-_{L_v}(g) = δ_{−1_n·𝒰_v×1_n}(g) … I_v(φ_v, φ′_v, f_v, χ) = volume(𝒰_v).”
sourceIssues.correction: Add to the conditions on L_v in §4.2.2 that χ_v(det(1_n − x)) = 1 for all x ∈ L_v, which is possible by shrinking L_v. Fix w := (−1_n, 1_n), or normalise f_{L_v} so that f^-_{L_v}(1) = 1. Then f^-_{L_v}|_{U_{1,v}×1_n} is the characteristic function of −1_n·𝒰_v × 1_n and I_v = vol(𝒰_v).
sourceIssues.reason: In (V_d, V^d)-coordinates (u, 1) = p^-·n(X), with p^- block lower triangular with upper-left block (u+1)/2 and X = (u+1)^{-1}(u−1), the Cayley transform. So (−u, 1) = (−1_n, 1_n)(u, 1) = (wp^-w^{-1})·w·n(X), with w = (−1_n, 1_n) and Δ(wp^-w^{-1}) = (u+1)/2 = (1_n − X)^{-1}. Hence f^-_{L_v}((u,1)) = f_{L_v}((−u,1)) = χ_v(det(1_n − X))^{-1}·|det(1_n − X)|^{s+n/2}·δ_{L_v}(X) = χ_v(det(1_n − X))^{-1}δ_{L_v}(X). The paper's two conditions on L_v (𝔘_v ⊇ N(L_v) and P_vwN(L_v) ⊆ P_v(−1_n K_v × 1_n)) do not make χ_v∘det trivial on 1 − L_v. If χ_v is ramified, I_v = ∫_{−𝒰_v} χ_v^{-1}(det(1 − X(u))) du can differ from vol(𝒰_v) and can even vanish. The paper never fixes w: it only says P_vw = P_v(−1_n, 1_n). If w = p_0(−1_n, 1_n) with p_0 ≠ 1, a constant character value χ_s(p_0) also appears. Defence: L_v is only asked to be ‘small enough’, so the extra condition changes nothing else, and later arguments only need I_v to be a nonzero constant. Independent check: The quotes on pp. 47–48 are accurate. The mistake is real. In polarization coordinates, (−1_n,1_n) = [[0,−1],[−1,0]] and (−u,1) = p·(−1_n,1_n)·n(X), where X = (1+u)^{-1}(u−1) and p has V^d-block Δ(p) = (1+u)/2 = (1−X)^{-1}. So with w = (−1_n,1_n), f^-_{L_v}((u,1)) = χ_v(det((1+u)/2))|det((1+u)/2)|^{…}δ_{L_v}(X) = χ_v(det(1−X))^{-1}δ_{L_v}(X) on the support. This is the characteristic function of −𝒰_v × 1 only if χ_v∘det is trivial on (1 − L_v)^{-1}. Neither stated condition on L_v (𝔘_v ⊇ N(L_v); P_vwN(L_v) ⊆ P_v(−1_nK_v × 1_n)) gives that, and K_v is chosen from φ_v, not from χ_v. For v ∈ S_χ ⊂ S′, I_v = ∫_{−𝒰_v} χ_v(det((1+u)/2))du, which can differ from vol(𝒰_v) and can vanish. A choice of w other than (−1_n,1_n) (the paper only has P_vw = P_v(−1_n,1_n)) adds a constant χ_s(p_0). Reach, changed from 'the proof': Lemma 4.2.3 itself asserts I_v = volume(𝒰_v) for L_v as constructed, and Theorem 4.6.1 states I_S = ∏_{v∈S}D_v(χ)·volume(𝒰_v). So stated results are false for some admissible L_v when χ_v is ramified. Both are repaired by the extra smallness condition (possible since L_v is at the authors' disposal) together with fixing w, or f^-_{L_v}(1) = 1. Same in v4 (p. 43) and v1 (p. 40).

sourceIssues.locator: §4.3.1, (54), p. 50, and the sentence following it (“Then, as explained in [Eis15], f_p ∈ I_p(χ_p, s).”), in arXiv v5
sourceIssues.printed: “f_{p,s}(g) = |ν|_p^{sn/2} ⊗_{w∈Σ_p} f_{w,s}(g_w), g = (ν, (g_w)) ∈ G(ℚ_p). (54) Then, as explained in [Eis15], f_p ∈ I_p(χ_p, s).”
sourceIssues.correction: (54) lies in I_p(χ_p, s) only after restriction to U_4(ℚ_p). To lie in I_p(χ_p, s) on all of G(ℚ_p), the factor |ν|_p^{sn/2} must be replaced by ∏_{w∈Σ_p} χ_{w̄}(ν)^n, reading the absolute values of §4.1.2 as the idelic module of 𝒦 (which makes the centre act unitarily). If |ν| is read as |ν|_{𝔸_ℚ}, the factor is instead |ν|_p^{sn/2}∏_{w∈Σ_p} χ_{w̄}(ν)^n |ν|_w^{-ns}.
sourceIssues.reason: For p = (ν, ((A_w, B_w; 0, D_w))_w) ∈ P(ℚ_p), the w̄-component of Δ(p) has determinant ν^n/det A_w, because V^d_{w̄} pairs with V_{d,w} and A_w·ᵗD_{w̄} = ν. Hence χ_p(det Δ(p)) = ∏_w χ_w(det D_w) χ_{w̄}^{-1}(det A_w) χ_{w̄}(ν)^n, while |det Δ(p)|_{𝒦_p}^{-s}|ν|_{𝒦_p}^{sn/2} = ∏_w |A_w^{-1}D_w|_w^{-s}. So I_p(χ_p, s) is induced from ∏_w ψ_{w,s}(p_w)·∏_w χ_{w̄}(ν)^n, whereas (54) transforms by |ν|_p^{sn/2}∏_w ψ_{w,s}(p_w). Test at s = 0 with a central element t = (t_w, t_{w̄}): I_p requires the factor χ_w(t_w)^n χ_{w̄}(t_{w̄})^n, and (54) gives χ_w(t_w)^n χ_{w̄}(t_w)^{-n}. These differ as soon as χ_{w̄}(t_w t_{w̄})^n ≠ 1. Defence: §4 only uses f_U, the restriction to U_4 (see (51)), where ν = 1 and (54) is correct. The similitude part matters only for the Eisenstein series on G_4 via [Eis15]. Independent check: The quote on p. 50 is accurate. For p = (ν,(p_w)) ∈ P(Q_p), unitarity of the similitude gives Δ_{w̄}(p) = ν·ᵗA_w^{-1}, since V^d_{w̄} pairs with V_{d,w}. Hence χ_p(det Δ(p)) = ∏_{w∈Σ_p} χ_w(det D_w)χ_{w̄}^{-1}(det A_w)χ_{w̄}(ν)^n. The factor χ_{w̄}(ν)^n cannot come from |ν|_p^{sn/2}. A decisive test at s = 0 with a central z = (z_w, z_{w̄}), ν = z_wz_{w̄}, which does not depend on how |·| is read: I_p needs the factor χ(z)^n = ∏χ_w(z_w)^nχ_{w̄}(z_{w̄})^n, while (54) gives ∏χ_w(z_w)^nχ_{w̄}(z_w)^{-n}. The ratio is ∏_wχ_{w̄}(ν)^n, which is nontrivial in general. So (54) is not in I_p(χ_p,s) on G(Q_p). It is in I_p after restriction to U_4 (ν = 1), which is all §4 uses through f_U and (51). The first reading's correction checks out: with |·| read as the K-idelic module, |det Δ|^{-s}|ν|^{sn/2} = ∏_w|A_w^{-1}D_w|^{-s}. Versions: v1 prints −sn/2 both globally and in (54). v4 prints +sn/2 globally and −sn/2 in (54). v5 prints +sn/2 in both.
searched: arXiv:1602.01776 v1 (February 2016), v2, v3 and v4 at the same place: v4 (4.3.1), p. 44 and v1–v3 print |ν|_p^{−sn/2}, also inconsistent. The global I(χ,s) had |ν|^{−sn/2} in v1–v3 and |ν|^{+sn/2} in v4–v5. So in v4 the global and local exponents disagreed, and v5 changed (54) to +sn/2 without adding χ_{w̄}(ν)^n.

sourceIssues.locator: §4.3.1, inequality (56), p. 51; used in Lemma 4.3.2(i),(ii), p. 52, and in the extension of μ′_w to Γ_R, ᵗΓ_R in §4.3.4, p. 55, in arXiv v5
sourceIssues.printed: “t ≥ max_{w∈Σ_p, 1≤i≤r(w)} (1, ord_w(cond(μ_{i,w})), ord_w(cond(χ_w)))), (56)”
sourceIssues.correction: t ≥ max_{w∈Σ_p, 1≤i≤r(w)} (1, ord_w(cond(μ_{i,w})), ord_w(cond(χ_w)), ord_{w̄}(cond(χ_{w̄}))), i.e. t must also bound the conductor of χ_{2,w} = χ_{w̄}^{-1}. With r ≥ 2t this also bounds the conductors of the μ′_{i,w}.
sourceIssues.reason: Lemma 4.3.2(i) and the support bounds in (ii) need every ν_{i,w} = χ_{1,w}^{-1}χ_{2,w}μ_{i,w} = χ_w^{-1}χ_{w̄}^{-1}μ_{i,w} to be trivial on 1 + 𝔭_w^t. The extension claim in §4.3.4 needs μ′_{i,w} = χ_{w̄}μ_{i,w}^{-1} (i ≤ t(w)) to be trivial on 1 + 𝔭^r. At split p, χ_w and χ_{w̄} are independent, and (56) does not bound cond(χ_{w̄}). Counterexample to Lemma 4.3.2(i): take n = 2, a_w = b_w = 1, so t(w) = 1, r(w) = 2, Γ_w(t) is the set of γ ∈ GL_2(O_w) diagonal mod 𝔭^t, and φ_ν((A, B; C, D)) = ν_1(A)ν_2(D) on 𝔛. With γ_1 = 1 and γ_2 = (1, ϖ^t; 0, 1), φ_ν(Xγ_2) = ν_1(A)ν_2(D + ϖ^tC) = ν_2(1 + ϖ^tC/D)φ_ν(X), while the right side of (i) is φ_ν(X) because μ_w(γ_2) = det γ_2 = 1. Suppose χ_w and μ_2 have conductor ≤ 𝔭^t and χ_{w̄} has conductor 𝔭^{t+1}. Then ν_2 is nontrivial on 1 + 𝔭^t and (i) fails for suitable C. Likewise φ(diag(α, 1)) need not be invariant under α ↦ α + 𝔭^tM, so supp Φ^{(1)} ⊆ 𝔭^{-t}M can fail. Defence: t (and r) are free, ‘sufficiently large’ parameters, so enlarging t repairs everything; possibly χ_w was meant to range over all w | p. Independent check: The quote of (56) on p. 51 is accurate. ν_{i,w} = χ_{1,w}^{-1}χ_{2,w}μ_{i,w} = χ_w^{-1}χ_{w̄}^{-1}μ_{i,w}, with χ_{w̄} viewed on K_w via K_w = K^+_{w+} = K_{w̄} (p. 49). (56) bounds cond(μ_{i,w}) and cond(χ_w) for w ∈ Σ_p only. I checked the counterexample. n = 2, a = b = 1, Γ_w(t) = matrices diagonal mod 𝔭^t, φ_ν((A B; C D)) = ν_1(A)ν_2(D) on 𝔛. γ_2 = (1 ϖ^t; 0 1) gives φ_ν(Xγ_2) = ν_2(1 + ϖ^tC/D)φ_ν(X), while the right side of Lemma 4.3.2(i) is φ_ν(X) (μ_w(γ_2) = 1, det γ_2 = 1). If cond χ_{w̄} = 𝔭^{t+1} and the other conductors are ≤ 𝔭^t, then ν_2 is nontrivial on 1+𝔭^t and (i) fails. The 𝔭^{-t} support bounds in (ii) fail with it. Likewise μ′_{i,w} = χ_{w̄}μ_{i,w}^{-1} (i ≤ t(w)) need not be trivial on 1+𝔭^r, so the extension of μ′_w to Γ_R, ᵗΓ_R on p. 55 is not justified by (56) and (60). Enlarging t repairs everything, since t and r are free. Identical in v4 ((4.3.3), p. 45) and v1.

sourceIssues.correction: In the V_w ⊕ V_w coordinates, an element of Hom(V_w, W_w) with components (Y_1, Y_2) has polarization components X_1 = (Y_1 − Y_2)/2 and X_2 = (Y_1 + Y_2)/2. So the function (58) is Φ_{χ,μ,w}(Y_1, Y_2) = vol(Γ_w)^{-1}Φ_{1,w}((Y_2 − Y_1)/2)Φ_{2,w}(Y_1 + Y_2). At (Y_1, Y_2) = (Xg, X)γ_V = ([Z′_1, Z″_2], [Z′_2, Z″_1]) this is not Vol(Γ_w)^{-1}Φ_{1,w}(Z′_1, Z″_2)Φ_{2,w}(Z′_2, Z″_1). One of two fixes is needed. Either §4.3.1 should define Φ_w := vol(Γ_w)^{-1}Φ_{1,w}(Y_1)Φ_{2,w}(Y_2) in V ⊕ V coordinates (for which §4.3.6–§4.3.10 are the correct computation), and its compatibility with the Eisenstein measure ([Eis15, Lemma 10], §5) must be re-established. Or §4.3.6–§4.3.10 must be redone for the section (58).
sourceIssues.reason: Coordinates: ι_d(a) + ι^d(b) = (a, −a) + (b, b) = (a + b, b − a), with V_d, V^d identified with V by the first projection (§4.1.1). Test case n = 1, a_w = 1, b_w = 0 (so γ_V = 1), with χ unramified at w and w̄, μ = μ_{1,w} ramified of conductor 𝔭^c (1 ≤ c ≤ t), β = π_w with β|_{O^×} = μ′ = μ^{-1}, and ν = μ on O^×. For the section (58), f((u,1)) = χ_2(u)|u|^{1/2+s} ∫ Φ_1(x(1−u)/2)Φ_2(x(1+u)) χ_1^{-1}χ_2(x)|x|^{1+2s} d^×x (up to vol(Γ_w)^{-1}). Since supp Φ_1 = O^× and supp Φ_2 = ϖ^{-c}O^×, the integrand vanishes unless |1 − u| = q^{-c}. Substitute z_1 = x(1−u)/2 ∈ O^× and z_2 = x(1+u) ∈ ϖ^{-c}O^×, so that d^×x d^×u = dz_1dz_2/|z_2|^2 and u = (z_2 − 2z_1)/(z_2 + 2z_1) ∈ 1 + 𝔭^c, on which βχ_2 = μ^{-1} is trivial. This gives Z_w = c′·∫_{O^×} μ(z_1) dz_1 · ∫ Φ_2(z_2)(χ_1^{-1}χ_2)(z_2/2)|z_2|^{2s−1} dz_2 = 0. The p. 59 formula instead gives Z_w = Vol^{-1}·vol(O^×)·∫ Φ_2(z)χ_1^{-1}β^{-1}(z)|z|^{s+1/2} d^×z = (nonzero constant)·(Gauss sum)·q^{c(s+1/2)} ≠ 0, in agreement with Theorem 4.3.10 (Z_w = ε(½ − s, π_a ⊗ χ_{1,w})·V_w·⟨φ_w, φ̃_w⟩, the L-factors being 1). So Theorem 4.3.10 does not compute the zeta integral of the section defined in (58). Defence: the paper is explicit that the V ⊕ V identification differs from the polarization one and rewrites 𝐗 correctly, and the §4.3.6–§4.3.10 computation is correct for the product function in V ⊕ V coordinates, which is presumably the intended section. The factor 2 in Φ_{2,w}(2X_2) turns into Φ_{2,w}(Y_1 + Y_2), so the authors may have had the coordinate change partly in mind. Marcil (arXiv:2311.05466, §4.1) makes the same step with his (37). Independent check: The quotes on pp. 52, 58 and 59 are accurate. §4.1.1 (p. 42): V_d = {(x,−x)} and V^d = {(x,x)}, identified with V by the first projection, and p. 50 builds the basis of W_w from these identifications. So an element with V⊕V components (Y_1,Y_2) has polarization components X_1 = (Y_1−Y_2)/2 and X_2 = (Y_1+Y_2)/2. This is consistent with p. 58's rewriting of 𝐗 = {(0,X)} as {(X,X)}. (58) is therefore Φ_w(Y_1,Y_2) = vol(Γ_w)^{-1}Φ_{1,w}((Y_2−Y_1)/2)Φ_{2,w}(Y_1+Y_2). From (73), (Xg,X)γ_V = ([Z′_1,Z″_2],[Z′_2,Z″_1]) (checked), so p. 59 evaluates Φ as vol^{-1}Φ_1(Y_1)Φ_2(Y_2). That is a different function, and no linear identification of V_d, V^d with V can make the two agree. I redid the n = 1, a_w = 1, b_w = 0 test (γ_V = 1; χ unramified at w and w̄; μ of conductor 𝔭^c, 1 ≤ c ≤ t; π_w a character equal to μ^{-1} on O^×). Φ_1 = μ·1_{O^×}, and Φ_2 is a Gauss-sum function supported on ϖ^{-c}O^×. For (58), Z_w ∝ ∫∫Φ_1(x(1−u)/2)Φ_2(x(1+u))χ_1^{-1}χ_2(x)|x|^{1+2s}χ_2π_w(u)|u|^{1/2+s}d^×xd^×u. On the support, |1+u| = 1 and u ∈ 1+𝔭^c, where π_wχ_2 = 1. The substitution z_1 = x(1−u)/2, z_2 = x(1+u) (Jacobian |x|) is a bijection onto O^× × ϖ^{-c}O^×, and the integral factors through ∫_{O^×}μ(z_1)dz_1 = 0. So Z_w ≡ 0. The p. 59 formula instead gives vol^{-1}·vol^×(O^×)·∫Φ_2(z)χ_1^{-1}π_w^{-1}(z)|z|^{s+1/2}d^×z ≠ 0. This agrees with Theorem 4.3.10, whose value is an ε-factor times 𝔙_w⟨φ_w,φ̃_w⟩, with trivial L-factors. So Theorem 4.3.10, and hence I_p in Theorem 4.6.1, does not hold for the section defined in (58). It is correct for the product section in V⊕V coordinates, whose relation to the Eisenstein measure ([Eis15, Lemma 10], partial Fourier transform in X_2) would have to be re-established. Versions: definition in v4 (p. 46) and v1 (p. 43). The evaluation in v4 (p. 52) and v1 (p. 47) is printed 'Φ((Xg, g))', so v4 also has that misprint. I did not check the first reading's remark about Marcil (arXiv:2311.05466). Second, independent reading of the same mistake: Toy case n = 1, a_w = 1, b_w = 0 (so γ_{V_w} = 1), K_w = Q_p with p odd, all finite-order characters trivial, t = 1, π_w unramified with π_w(p) = α, X := q^{−(s+1/2)}. Then Φ_1 = char(O^×) and Φ_2 = char_O − q^{−1}char_{p^{−1}O}. With the product function Φ' one gets Z = (1 − αq^{−1}X^{−1})/(1 − α^{−1}X) = L(s + 1/2, π̃)/L(1/2 − s, π), as Theorem 4.3.10 predicts. With the literal Φ_w of §4.3.1 one gets Z = (1 − q^{−1})[α^{−1}X/(1 − α^{−1}X) + αX/(1 − αX) + (q − 2)/(q − 1)] − q^{−2}X^{−2}, which also has the pole of L(s + 1/2, π). I confirmed both closed forms by exact enumeration modulo p^5 for p = 3. So the two sections really differ, and Theorem 4.3.10 is about the translated section. Even if Φ is read in the new coordinates, the p. 59 formula also drops the unit constants coming from −X_1 and 2X_2 (∏_iμ_{i,w}(−1)^{n_{i,w}} and ∏_iν_{i,w}(2)^{−n_{i,w}}) and the factor χ_{2,w}(det γ_{V_w}) = χ_{2,w}(−1)^{b_w}. Case for the defence: the authors say explicitly that they switch decompositions ('often convenient … e.g. in [GPSR87]'). v1 (p. 46, (4.3.10)) put an extra change-of-basis-type matrix (½·1_n, −½·1_n; 1_n, 1_n) into the translation, so the need for a translation was recognised. The discrepancy is a right translation of the section by a fixed group element together with unit constants, so the shape of the Euler factor is unaffected provided the Eisenstein measure is built from the matching section. Marcil (arXiv:2311.05466, (37) and p. 23) repeats the same step, also dropping the sign −X_1. Independent check: Quotations checked on the page images (pp. 50, 52, 58-59). By §4.1.1 (p. 42), V^d = {(x,x)} and V_d = {(x,-x)}, and both are identified with V by the first projection (p. 50 uses the same identification for the matrices X_1, X_2). So a homomorphism with V+V components (Y_1,Y_2) has polarization components X_1 = (Y_1-Y_2)/2 and X_2 = (Y_1+Y_2)/2. Then (58) is Phi(Y) = vol^-1 Phi_1((Y_2-Y_1)/2) Phi_2(Y_1+Y_2). It is not the product vol^-1 Phi_1(Y_1)Phi_2(Y_2) that the p. 59 display uses. The block bookkeeping (Xg,X)gamma = ([Z_1',Z_2''],[Z_2',Z_1'']) is itself correct. I re-derived the toy case by hand: n=a=1, b=0, K_w=Q_p with p odd, trivial characters, t=1, pi unramified with pi(p)=alpha, and X=q^-(s+1/2). The product function gives (1-alpha q^-1 X^-1)/(1-alpha^-1 X) = L(s+1/2,pi~)/L(1/2-s,pi), as Theorem 4.3.10 predicts. The literal (58) needs |z_2-z_1|=1 and splits into four cases: v(z_1)=0<v(z_2); v(z_2)=0<v(z_1); z_1,z_2 units with z_1 !≡ z_2 mod p; and v(z_1)=v(z_2)=-1 with z_1≡z_2 mod p but not mod p^2. These give (1-q^-1)[alpha^-1X/(1-alpha^-1X)+alphaX/(1-alphaX)+(q-2)/(q-1)] - q^-2 X^-2. I reran the exact-enumeration check (p=3, mod 3^5), and it matches both closed forms up to truncation (-3.9487 vs -3.9487; -4.798 vs -4.793). A second test, the ramified case of sourceIssues E52 (n=a=1, b=0, chi unramified, mu of conductor p^c): the supports force u=z_1/z_2 in 1+p^c, and the literal zeta integral then contains the factor ∫_{O^x} mu = 0. Theorem 4.3.10 instead gives eps(1/2-s, pi_a⊗chi_1)·Vol·<phi,phi~>, which is nonzero. Theorem 4.3.10 is stated for Z_w built from the translate (73) of the section (58), and (58) is the p-adic section fed into Definition 5.3.2 (p. 85: 'choices ... 4.3 (local choices for v | p)'). So the theorem is false as stated for the section the paper defines. This is an error in a stated result, not only a gap in the proof, and it agrees with sourceIssues E52. The §4.3.6-4.3.10 computation is correct for the product Schwartz function in V_w+V_w coordinates. Whether the Main Theorem survives depends on the Eisenstein measure ([Eis15], Theorem 8.2.2) being built from that section. In the ramified test the literal section would make the p-adic L-function vanish at those characters. Smaller slips: the unit constants from -X_1 and 2X_2 and the factor chi_2(det gamma) = chi_2(-1)^{b_w} are also dropped (p. 58 writes chi_2(g), not chi_2(det g·gamma)). Versions: v4 p. 52 prints 'Phi((Xg,g))'. v1 (4.3.10) puts an extra matrix (1/2, -1/2; 1, 1) into the translation, but v1 (4.3.12) still evaluates Phi((Xg,X)gamma) without it, so v1 was already inconsistent. Reach: a stated result (whether the section whose zeta integral is computed is the section (58) used in the Eisenstein measure).

sourceIssues.locator: Proposition 4.3.7, second statement (77), p. 60, and its proof pp. 60–61, in arXiv v5; present in v4 pp. 53–54
sourceIssues.printed: “When all of the above conditions are met, we have the following factorization at each prime w ∈ Σ_p: Φ_{1,w}(Z_1', Z_2'')Φ_{2,w}(Z_2', Z_1'')⟨π_w(Z_1)φ_w, π̃_w(Z_2)φ̃_w⟩_{π_w} = Vol(Γ_{a_w,b_w})·J_1·J_2” (conditions: A_1 ∈ Γ_{a_w,w}(t), C_1 ∈ p_w^t M, D_2 ∈ Γ_{b_w,w}(t), B_2 ∈ p_w^t M, …); proof: “π_w(Z_1)φ_w = π_w((1 0; C_1 D_1))μ'_w((A_1 0; 0 1))φ_w, π̃_w(Z_2)φ̃_w = π̃_w((A_2 B_2; 0 1))(μ'_w)^{−1}((1 0; 0 D_2))φ̃_w” and, on p. 61, “A = 1 − B_2C_1 ∈ 1 + p_w^{2t}M_{a_w}(O_w) … D = (1 + CB_2)D_1 ∈ (1 + p^{2t}M_{b_w}(O_w))D_1. Therefore, applying the invariance conditions (66) and (69) we obtain ⟨π_w((1 0; C_1 D_1))φ_w, π̃_w((A_2 B_2; 0 1))φ̃_w⟩ = ⟨π_w((1 −B_2; 0 1)(1 0; C_1 D_1))φ_w, π̃_w((A_2 0; 0 1))φ̃_w⟩ = ⟨π_w((1 0; C_1 1)(1 0; 0 D_1))φ_w, π̃_w(A_2 0; 0 1)φ̃_w⟩ = …”
sourceIssues.correction: (77) holds only under the extra conditions A_1 in Gamma_{a_w,w}, D_2 in Gamma_{b_w,w} (level p^r) and r = 2t (or with the factors A = 1-B_2C_1 and 1+CB_2 carried along). State Proposition 4.3.7 in that form, and prove Corollary 4.3.8 by first using the Gamma_w(t)-invariance of the integrand of (74) to reduce to that case, as in the first reading's steps (i)-(iii).
sourceIssues.reason: (66) and (69) give equivariance only under Γ_{R,w}, ᵗΓ_{R,w}, which have level p^r with r ≥ 2t (60). The support of Φ_{1,w} = Γ_w(t) gives only level p^t. So diag(A_1, 1) with A_1 ∈ Γ_{a_w,w}(t) \ Γ_{a_w,w} need not act on φ_w by μ'_w. For example, for u lower unipotent with entries in p^t \ p^r, π_{a_w}(u)φ_{a_w} ≠ φ_{a_w}, since the model function of φ_{a_w} is supported on B_{a_w}Γ_{a_w,w}. In the p. 61 chain the second equality silently replaces (1 0; C 1)(A 0; 0 D) by (1 0; C_1 1)(1 0; 0 D_1). Carrying the factors through gives ⟨φ_w, π̃_w(diag(A^{−1}A_2, D_1^{−1}(1 + CB_2)^{−1}))φ̃_w⟩. Removing A^{−1} and (1 + CB_2)^{−1} needs diag(A, 1) ∈ Γ_{R,w} and diag(1, 1 + CB_2) ∈ ᵗΓ_{R,w}, i.e. 1 + p^{2t}M ⊂ Γ(r), i.e. r ≤ 2t. The next step (levi-coefficient-factorization) needs r ≥ 2t (D_1CA_2 ∈ O for C ∈ p^r). So the printed argument covers exactly r = 2t. Case for the defence: the final formulas (Corollary 4.3.8, Theorem 4.3.10) do hold, and the missing steps are routine once noticed. Marcil 2023 (Lemma 4.1, Lemma 4.2, Proposition 4.3) takes Φ_{1,w} of level p^r and handles the elements γ_0 = (A, AB; 0, 1), γ̃_0 = (1, 0; C, 1 + CB_2) explicitly, which avoids the issue. Independent check: Quotations checked on pp. 60-61. First step of the proof: it applies (66) to diag(A_1,1). But Prop. 4.3.7 only gives A_1 in Gamma_{a_w,w}(t) (level p^t, from supp Phi_{1,w} = Gamma_w(t), p. 51), while (66) holds on Gamma_{R,w} (level p^r, r >= 2t). Second step: the second equality of the p. 61 chain needs diag(A,1) in Gamma_R and diag(1,1+CB_2) in tGamma_R, where A = 1-B_2C_1 = (1+B_2C)^-1 is in 1+p^{2t}M. That requires r <= 2t, while the Levi step needs D_1CA_2 integral, i.e. r >= 2t. So the printed argument covers at most r = 2t, and even there the A_1 problem remains. Beyond the proof, (77) itself is false as stated. Counterexample: b_w=0, a_w=n=2, partition 1+1, K_w=Q_p, all characters trivial, pi_{i,w} unramified, t=1, r=2. Let phi = char(B·Iw_2), where Iw_2 has lower-left entry in p^2. Let phi~ be supported on B·tIw_2 with phi~(k) = [k_22 in O^x] on GL_2(O); it satisfies (67) and (69). Take A_1 = u = (1 0; p 1), which is in Gamma_{a,w}(1), and A_2 = diag(p^-1, p), which is in p^-1 M_2(O). Then Phi^(1)(A_2) = -(1-1/p)/p ≠ 0. Next, <pi(u)phi, pi~(A_2)phi~> = ∫_{k_22 unit} phi(k A_2^-1 u) dk = 0: the bottom row of kA_2^-1u is (p k_21 + k_22, p^-1 k_22), whose ratio has valuation 1. On the other hand <phi, pi~(A_2)phi~> ≠ 0 (the ratio is p^2k_21/k_22). So the left side of (77) is 0, while the right side Vol·Phi^(1)(A_2)·<phi_a, pi~_a(A_2)phi~_a> is nonzero. Corollary 4.3.8 survives. The integrand of (74) is invariant under (Z_1,Z_2) -> (uZ_1,uZ_2) for unipotent u in Gamma_w(t), by Lemma 4.3.2(i) (for Phi_2) and the definition of Phi_1, and this reduces A_1 to level p^r. I checked this step (the first reading's step (i)); steps (ii)-(iii) for the A and 1+CB_2 factors are plausible but I did not check them. So the false statement is (77) of Prop. 4.3.7; Corollary 4.3.8 and Theorem 4.3.10 are not affected by it. v4 pp. 53-54 has the same text.

Also Vol(Γ_{R,w})/Vol(Γ_{R,w} ∩ ᵗΓ_{R,w}) = [Γ_{R,w} : Γ_{R,w} ∩ ᵗΓ_{R,w}] = |N_{R_w}(O_w/p_w^r)| = q_w^{r·dim N_{R_w}}, since Γ_{R,w} ∩ ᵗΓ_{R,w} is the set of matrices that are in the Levi L_{R_w} mod p^r. This is positive-dimensional unless R_w = GL_n. Case for the defence: the claim becomes true if the test vectors are renormalized so that ⟨φ_w, φ̃_w⟩ is proportional to Vol(Γ_{R,w} ∩ ᵗΓ_{R,w}), which may be what the global normalization of §8–§9 achieves (Main Theorem 9.2.2 asserts that Ω_{π',χ} = ⟨φ, φ^♭_χ⟩/(Vol(I^0_{r_1,V} ∩ I^0_{r_1,−V})Q) is independent of r_1). Gamma_R ∩ tGamma_R is the preimage of the Levi L_R(O/p^r), and tR is the opposite parabolic, so Vol(Gamma_R)/Vol(Gamma_R ∩ tGamma_R) = |N_R(O/p^r)| = q^{r·dim N_R}. The right-hand side of the remark is therefore L·q^{r dim N_R}·prod<phi_i,phi~_i>, which depends on r unless N_R = 1. The left-hand side (by (83) as printed, or as corrected in sourceIssues E58) also depends on r. sourceIssues.locator: Corollary 4.4.9, last statement, and its proof, p. 73, in arXiv v5; present in v4 pp. 64–65
sourceIssues.printed: “Then for all κ† ≤ κ there exist unique elements δ(κ, κ†) ∈ U(p^+_3), defined over algebraic number fields, such that D(κ, χ) = Σ_{κ†≤κ} δ(κ, κ†) ∘ D^{hol}(κ†, χ); δ(κ, κ) is the scalar ∏_σ P_{κ_σ,χ,σ}.” … “The remaining statements are formal consequences of the decomposition (93) and the fact that the decomposition is rational over an appropriate reflex field, cf. Lemma 7.3.2 of [Har86].”
sourceIssues.correction: An argument is needed that the component of D(κ, χ)v(χ) in each summand D(κ†) ⊗ D(κ†^♭ ⊗ χ) lies in U(p^+_3)·(v_{κ†} ⊗ v_{κ†^♭⊗χ}). Alternatively, δ(κ, κ†) should be allowed to be vector-valued differential operators, i.e. elements of U(p^+_3) composed with maps between K_3-types.
sourceIssues.reason: Each summand is U(p^+_3) ⊗ (minimal K_3-type), and U(p^+_3)·(v ⊗ v) consists of the vectors whose K_3-type component is the highest-weight line. The component of δ(r̃, s̃)·v(χ) in the κ†-summand is a K_3-highest-weight vector of weight κ in S(p^+_3) ⊗ W_{κ†}. When W_{κ†} has dimension > 1 such a vector is in general a combination Σ p_i ⊗ w_i with w_i of lower weight, not of the form p ⊗ v_{κ†}, so neither existence nor the meaning of 'δ(κ, κ†) ∘ D^{hol}(κ†, χ)' follows formally. Case for the defence: with vector-valued operators the decomposition is immediate from (93). The only use, in §8.1 (Proposition 8.1.3 and the proof of Corollary 8.2.4, 'by induction on the size of κ'), needs just that the terms with κ† ≠ κ are killed by the ordinary projector, which holds for such operators as well. The meaning of the order κ† ≤ κ is not explained either. I did not settle this. Independent check: Checked p. 73. The kappa†-component of D(kappa,chi)v(chi) is a K_3-highest-weight vector of weight kappa in D(kappa†)⊗D(kappa†^flat⊗chi), which is S(p_3^+)⊗W_{kappa†}⊗W_{kappa†^flat} as a K_3-module. Writing it as delta(kappa,kappa†)·(v⊗v) with delta in U(p_3^+) requires it to lie in S(p_3^+)⊗(highest-weight line). This is automatic when the minimal K-types are 1-dimensional (e.g. a_sigma, b_sigma <= 1). In general it is not a formal consequence of (93), and for non-Cartan constituents it is not expected. The paper itself stresses, just before, that delta(r~,s~)v(chi) need not lie in the highest-weight space. So 'formal consequences' does not prove the statement as formulated. With vector-valued operators the decomposition does follow, and the first reading reports that the §8.1 uses need only that the terms with kappa† ≠ kappa are killed by the ordinary projector; I did not re-check those uses. v4 pp. 64-65 is the same. sourceIssues.locator: §4.4.12, p. 75, first sentence, in arXiv v5; present in v4 p. 66 and v2/v3 p. 66
sourceIssues.printed: “If π is a cuspidal automorphic representation of GU(V) whose component at σ is an anti-holomorphic discrete series representation of the form D_c(τ_σ), then its base change Π to an automorphic representation of GL(n)_K (ignoring the split center) is cuspidal, cohomological, and satisfies Π^∨ ≅ Π^c”
sourceIssues.correction: Π is an isobaric sum of conjugate-self-dual cuspidal representations (cohomological, Π^∨ ≅ Π^c). It is cuspidal only for π with stable (non-endoscopic) parameter.
sourceIssues.reason: Endoscopic cuspidal representations of unitary groups, e.g. those whose parameter is a sum of two conjugate-self-dual parameters, have non-cuspidal base change (Mok, KMSW). Case for the defence: the passage is motivational ('in most cases'), and the Hodge types (106) depend only on the archimedean component. Independent check: Checked p. 75. Base change of a cuspidal representation of a unitary group is in general only an isobaric sum of conjugate-self-dual cuspidal representations. Endoscopic cuspidal representations can have discrete series at infinity: for example, holomorphic CM forms on U(1,1) have base change Ind of characters, and Rogawski's endoscopic packets on U(2,1) contain holomorphic discrete series members. The paper itself writes in Remark 9.3.2 'an automorphic representation ... whose base change to GL(n) is cuspidal', which acknowledges that this is an extra condition. v4 p. 66 is the same. Reach: nothing (expository).

sourceIssues.locator: §4.4.14, p. 76, and §4.5.4, p. 76 versus Proposition 4.5.6, p. 77, in arXiv v5; present in v4 pp. 67–68
sourceIssues.printed: §4.4.14: “with φ_v a vector in the minimal U_σ-type 1 ⊗ W^∨_{τ_σ} of D_c(κ) … φ_{κ,+} (resp. φ_{κ,−}) is an eigenvector for T_σ of weight −w_0(κ) (resp. of weight −κ).” §4.5.4: “Let φ_σ ⊗ φ^♭_σ be an anti-holomorphic vector in the highest weight subspace of the minimal K_σ-type of π_σ ⊗ π^♭_σ.” Proposition 4.5.6: “where φ_σ = φ_{κ_σ,−}, φ^♭_σ = φ_{κ^♭_σ,−}”
sourceIssues.correction: By (90) and §4.4.1, the minimal U_σ-type of D_c(κ) is 1 ⊗ W_{τ_σ}. Either §4.4.1/(90) or §4.4.14 must be adjusted, together with the weights. The vector used in Propositions 4.5.5 and 4.5.6 should be described consistently: the lowest weight vector φ_{κ,−} in Proposition 4.5.6 and (50), but 'highest weight subspace' in §4.5.4.
sourceIssues.reason: (90) gives D_c(τ_σ) = U(𝔤_σ) ⊗_{U(k_σ⊕p^+_σ)} W_{τ_σ}, and p. 67 states that its minimal U_σ-type is 1 ⊗ W_{τ_σ}. For the pairing in Proposition 4.5.5 to be non-zero the anti-holomorphic vector must be dual to the highest weight vector v_κ ⊗ v_{κ^♭⊗χ} of the holomorphic side, i.e. the lowest weight vector of the dual type, consistent with φ_{κ,−}. Case for the defence: the inconsistency is between two dual conventions and the intended vector is clear from (50) and Proposition 4.5.6.

sourceIssues.locator: Lemma 4.5.2 and §4.5.4, (107), p. 76, in arXiv v5 (with §4.4.2, p. 69); present in v4 p. 67
sourceIssues.printed: Lemma 4.5.2: “ι(m, χ_σ)(D²(m, χ_σ)) ⊂ I_σ(m − n/2, χ).” §4.5.4: “f_σ = f_σ(χ_σ, c) ∈ I(χ_{u,σ}, m) … f_σ(χ_σ, c, g) = B(χ_σ, κ_σ)D(κ_σ, m, χ_{u,σ})J_{m,χ_{u,σ}}(g) … where J_{m,χ_{u,σ}} ∈ C^∞(G_4) is the canonical automorphy factor introduced in Section 4.4.2”
sourceIssues.correction: Fix one parametrization. J_χ and D²(m, χ_0) of §4.4.2 use χ = ||•||^m χ_0 with χ_{0,σ}(z) = z^{−a}z̄^{−b} algebraic, whereas §4.5.4 and §4.6 use χ = ||•||^m χ_u with χ_u unitary. The two m differ by (a(χ_σ) + b(χ_σ))/2; §5.3.1 calls the first one μ. Say which induced representation, I(χ, s) or I(χ_u, s), and which s contains the image of ι.
sourceIssues.reason: With the same letter m used for both factorizations and the argument order of I_σ(·, ·) swapped relative to §4.1.2, one cannot tell which section (107) denotes. Lemma 4.5.2 (proof omitted: 'an easy computation, similar to that in [Har97]') places the image in I_σ(m − n/2, χ), while §4.5.4 and Definition 5.3.2 place f_σ in I(χ_{u,σ}, m). I could not reconcile these without the paper's sign conventions for the tube-domain realization, so I did not verify Lemma 4.5.2. Case for the defence: §5.3.1 explicitly separates μ from m ('We omit the expression of μ and χ_0 in terms of m and χ_u'), so the authors were aware of the two normalizations. Independent check: Checked pp. 69, 76, 83-84. §4.4.2 defines J_{chi_sigma} = J_{m,chi_0} for chi = ||·||^m chi_0 with chi_{0,sigma} = z^-a zbar^-b algebraic. Lemma 4.5.2 puts the image of iota(m,chi_sigma) in I_sigma(m - n/2, chi), with the arguments in the reverse order to §4.1.2's I(chi,s). §4.5.4, (107) and Definition 5.3.2 instead put f_sigma = B·D(kappa,m,chi_{u,sigma})J_{m,chi_{u,sigma}} in I(chi_{u,sigma}, m), where chi = ||·||^m chi_u with chi_u unitary; so J_{m,chi_u} is used with a unitary chi_u, although J was defined for algebraic chi_0. I(chi,s) and I(chi_u,s') differ by a shift of s depending on the factorization, so the two placements cannot both hold with the same m. §5.3.1 introduces mu to separate the two normalizations and says 'We omit the expression of mu and chi_0 in terms of m and chi_u'. The global identity (Theorem 4.6.1) needs all local sections in the same I(chi_u,m), and the proof of Lemma 4.5.2 is omitted, so which section (107) denotes is not established. v4 p. 67 is the same. Reach: the proof (identification of the archimedean section).

sourceIssues.locator: Proposition 4.5.6, p. 77, in arXiv v5; present in v4 p. 68
sourceIssues.printed: “In the meantime, we will be satisfied with the following result, due to Garrett [Gar08]. Proposition 4.5.6. … Then I_σ(χ_σ, κ_σ) is a non-zero algebraic number.”
sourceIssues.correction: Non-vanishing follows from Proposition 4.5.5. For algebraicity the text itself only reports that [Gar08] proves the integrals 'algebraic up to a predictable power of the transcendental number π, which can be normalized away', for F imaginary quadratic (Remark 4.5.7). The statement needs the normalization (Haar measure at σ and/or the constant B(χ_σ, κ_σ) of (107)) that removes this power of π, and a reference or proof for general CM K.
sourceIssues.reason: The paragraph before the proposition says Garrett shows algebraicity 'up to a predictable power of … π', and explicit values are known only when one factor of the extreme K-type is one-dimensional ([Gar08, p. 12]). Remark 4.5.7 says the computation in [Har08, §5] is for imaginary quadratic F and 'the same reasoning applies in general'. B(χ_σ, κ_σ) is only required to be a non-zero algebraic scalar, so it cannot absorb a power of π. Case for the defence: only non-vanishing (and algebraicity up to an explicit normalization) is needed for the construction, and Eischen–Liu (arXiv:2006.04302) later computed these integrals. Independent check: Checked p. 77. The paragraph before the proposition says that Garrett shows the integrals are 'algebraic up to a predictable power of the transcendental number pi, which can be normalized away', gives exact values only when one factor of the extreme K-type is one-dimensional, and gives non-zero algebraic values when both are scalar. Remark 4.5.7 relies on [Har08] for imaginary quadratic F ('the same reasoning applies in general'). The proposition asserts plain algebraicity without fixing the Haar measure or normalizing constant that removes the power of pi. B(chi_sigma,kappa_sigma) is now required to be algebraic (v5 p. 76; v4 said only 'non-zero scalar'), so it cannot absorb a power of pi. Non-vanishing follows from Proposition 4.5.5. Reach: a stated result (the algebraicity part of Proposition 4.5.6).

sourceIssues.reason: By (83), the local factor at w is L(s + 1/2, ord, π_w, χ_w). The global identity is evaluated at the same s as L^S(s + 1/2, …). Main Theorem 9.2.2 inherits the shift ('L_p(m, ord, π', χ_u) L^S(m + 1/2, π', χ_u)'). Marcil 2023, Theorem 4.6, writes E_p(s + 1/2, P − ord, π_p, χ_p). Case for the defence: this is a pure naming shift, and L_p(s, ord) could be read as 'the ord-factor attached to the value at s + 1/2'. Independent check: Checked p. 64 and p. 78. (83) says 'L(s+1/2, ord, pi_w, chi_w) is the ratio ... that appear in the formula for Z_w', which defines L(·,ord) with the shift built in. Remark 4.3.11 also calls prod_w L(s+1/2,ord,...) the Euler factor at p. Theorem 4.6.1 instead sets I_p = L_p(s,ord) := prod_w L(s,ord,pi_w,chi_w), in the same identity as L^S(s+1/2). Main Theorem 9.2.2 inherits this as 'L_p(m,ord,pi',chi_u) L^S(m+1/2,...)'. Also I_inf(chi,rho^upsilon) and I_inf(chi,kappa) denote the same product. v4 p. 69 is the same. Reach: a stated result (by a shift of 1/2 in the argument of the p-factor). Second, independent reading of the same mistake: (83) (p. 64) gives the p-adic zeta integral as I_w = L(s + 1/2, ord, π_w, χ_w)·𝔙_w·⟨φ_w, φ̃_w⟩, and (86) displays this ratio with arguments s + 1/2 and −s + 1/2; Theorem 4.6.1 (p. 78) nevertheless sets L_p(s, ord, π, χ) := ∏_{w|p} L(s, ord, π_w, χ_w) and uses it in I_p at the same s, a half-unit shift; specialising s = m produces L_p(m, …) in the Main Theorem, next to L^S(m + 1/2, …). Defence: the Main Theorem is consistent with Theorem 4.6.1's own (misprinted) definition; the intended meaning is clear from (83), (86) and the parallel L^S(m + 1/2). Independent check: Checked on the page images (pp. 64–65, 78, 145). (83) defines L(s+1/2, ord, π_w, χ_w) as the ratio of L- and ε-factors in Z_w, whose arguments are s+1/2 and −s+1/2 ((86)). Remark 4.3.11 calls ∏_{w|p}L(s+1/2,ord,π_w,χ_w) 'the Euler factor at p'. Theorem 4.6.1 nevertheless defines L_p(s,ord,π,χ) := ∏_w L(s,ord,π_w,χ_w) and puts L_p(s,…) into I_p at the same s as L^S(s+1/2,π,χ_u), a half-unit shift. Specializing at s = m gives L_p(m,ord,π′,χ_u) next to L^S(m+1/2,π′,χ_u) in the Main Theorem. The intended value is L_p(m+1/2,…), i.e. ∏_w L(m+1/2,ord,π′_w,χ_{u,w}). Intended meaning clear from (83), (86) and the parallel L^S(m+1/2). Versions: v4 same; v2/v3 also have I_p = L_p(s,ord,π,χ) and L_p(m,ord,π,χ_u) in the Main Theorem.
searched: arXiv:1602.01776 v1 (February 2016), v2, v3 and v4 at the same place: v4 p. 69 same; v2/v3 Proposition 4.6.1 (p. 68–69): 'I_p = L_p(s, ord, π, χ) := ∏_{w|p} L(s, ord, π_w, χ_w)' with (4.3.24) defining L(s + 1/2, ord, π_w, χ_w), so the shift is present from v2. Same in v4 ((83) = (4.3.30) on p. 57, Theorem 4.6.1 on p. 69, Main Theorem p. 134).

sourceIssues.locator: Theorem 4.6.1, p. 78, in arXiv v5; present in v4 p. 69 and v2/v3 (Proposition 4.6.1)
sourceIssues.printed: “Assume the local components at finite places outside S = S_π are unramified vectors … assume the Siegel–Weil section f_s ∈ I(χ, s) … Write χ = ||•||^m χ_u. Then we have the equality D(χ)·I(φ, φ^♭, f, s) = ⟨φ, φ^♭⟩ · I_p(χ, κ)I_∞(χ, ρ^υ)I_S L^S(s + 1/2, π, χ_u) where I_S = ∏_{v∈S} D_v(χ)·volume(𝒰_v)”
sourceIssues.correction: D(χ) · I(φ, φ^♭, f, m) = ⟨φ, φ^♭⟩ · ∏_{v|p}D_v(χ) · I_p · I_∞ · I_{S'} · L^{S'∪Σ_p}(m + 1/2, π, χ_u), for f ∈ I(χ_u, m) (equivalently D^{Σ_p}(χ)·I = ⟨φ, φ^♭⟩ I_p I_∞ I_{S'} L^{S'∪Σ_p}(m + 1/2, π, χ_u)), where S' ⊇ S_π ∪ S_χ ∪ S_K is the set of places of §4.2 and I_{S'} = ∏_{v∈S'}D_v(χ)vol(U_v).
sourceIssues.reason: The unfolding gives I = ⟨φ, φ^♭⟩∏_v I_v. For v ∉ S' ∪ Σ_p, d_{n,v}(s, χ_v)I_v = L_v(s + 1/2, π_v, χ_v) (§4.2.1), and d_{n,v}(s, χ_{u,v}) = D_v(χ) only at s = m (definition (108): D_v(χ) = d_{n,v}(m, χ_v)). So the identity holds at s = m for sections in I(χ_u, m), the parametrization used in Definition 5.3.2 and Corollary 9.1.8, not for f_s ∈ I(χ, s) with variable s. For v | p, I_v = I_w is given by Theorem 4.3.10, which contains no standard Euler factor and no D_v. So the D_v(χ) (v | p) contained in D(χ) = D^∅(χ) have no counterpart on the right, and L^S (S = S_π, which does not contain p when π_p is unramified) wrongly includes the Euler factors at p. Moreover the unramified computation needs v ∉ S_ram = S_π ∪ S_χ ∪ S_K, and Lemma 4.2.3 is stated for v ∈ S', so S should be S', not S_π. If instead p ∈ S_π, then I_S would include p-adic places with the §4.2.2 value D_v·vol(U_v), which is not what is computed at p. Case for the defence: it is plausible that the intended statement omits the places above p from both D(χ) and L^S (the natural shape for a p-adic L-function, with the modified factor L_p(ord) replacing the Euler factor at p). But the printed formula does not say so, and Corollary 9.1.8 and Main Theorem 9.2.2 reproduce it (with D(χ) and L^S). Independent check: Checked p. 78, p. 47 ((53)), §4.2 (p. 46), Corollary 9.1.8 and Main Theorem 9.2.2 (pp. 144-145). (i) The s-dependence. D_v(chi) = prod_r L_v(2m+n-r, chi^+ eta^r) = d_{n,v}(m, chi_{u,v}) is fixed by m. For f in I(chi,s) with chi = ||·||^m chi_u, the unramified factor is L_v(s+1/2,pi,chi) = L_v(s+m+1/2,pi,chi_u) over d_{n,v}(s,chi) = d_{n,v}(s+m,chi_u). So the printed identity (D(chi) on the left, L^S(s+1/2,pi,chi_u) on the right) can hold only at s = m for sections in I(chi_u,m), which is the parametrization of Definition 5.3.2 and Corollary 9.1.8. (ii) The places above p. D(chi) = D^∅(chi) runs over all finite v, including v|p (108). The factor I_p of Theorem 4.3.10 contains no D_v, and at v|p the section is not unramified. S = S_pi need not contain p (§4.2 even requires p not in S), so L^S wrongly keeps the Euler factor at p. The printed identity is off by prod_{v|p} L_v(m+1/2,pi,chi_u)/D_v(chi), which is not 1 when chi is unramified at p. (iii) At places of S_chi ∪ S_K outside S_pi the sections are those of §4.2.2, with I_v = vol(U_v), so the set should be S' as in §4.2. Main Theorem 9.2.2 reproduces D(chi) (via Corollary 9.1.8) and L^S. v4 p. 69 is the same. Reach: a stated result (Theorem 4.6.1; through Corollary 9.1.8, the form of Main Theorem 9.2.2).

sourceIssues.locator: §5.1, p. 79, after the definition of Λ_{X,R}, in arXiv v5
sourceIssues.printed: Λ_{X,R} = lim_i R[X/X_i]. This is a compact topological ring.
sourceIssues.correction: This is a topological ring, compact when R is compact (e.g. R finite over Z_p).
sourceIssues.reason: For a general p-adic ring R (e.g. R = O_{C_p}, or R = Z_p[[T]] with its p-adic topology, both allowed in §5.1) R[X/X_i] ≅ R^{#(X/X_i)} is not compact, and neither is the inverse limit. Defence: compactness is never used. Independent check: Checked p. 79. R is any 'p-adic ring' (p-adic topology). For R = O_{C_p}, allowed since R ⊂ C_p is used throughout, R itself is not compact (its residue field is infinite), and Lambda_{X,R} for X trivial is R. Compactness holds when R is compact, e.g. finite over Z_p, and it is never used. v4 is the same.
searched: arXiv:1602.01776 v1 (February 2016), v2, v3 and v4 at the same place: Same in v4 (p. 78) and v2/v3 (p. 78).

sourceIssues.locator: §5.3.1, p. 84, paragraph after Definition 5.3.2, in arXiv v5
sourceIssues.printed: One obtains a measure normalized at S from an unnormalized measure by multiplying by the appropriate product of local Euler factors at S.
sourceIssues.correction: Multiplying by chi -> prod_{v in S} D_v(chi) gives a pseudo-measure; it is a measure when the elements 1 - eta^r(varpi_v) q_v^{r-n}[varpi_v] (v in S, 0 <= r <= n-1) are units in Lambda_{X_p}. Otherwise state the Main Theorem with the unnormalized measure (I_S = prod_{v in S} vol(U_v)), or in the localized Iwasawa algebra.
sourceIssues.reason: For v ∈ S (v ∤ p) at which χ is unramified, D_v(χ) = ∏_r (1 − η^r(ϖ_v) q_v^{r−n} χ(ϖ_v))^{-1}, the evaluation at χ of the inverse of an element of the Iwasawa algebra Λ_{X_p}; that element is a unit only if its reductions at all maximal ideals are non-zero, which fails e.g. for r = n−1 when q_v ≡ ±1 (mod p) and the residual image of [ϖ_v] allows η^r(ϖ_v) q_v^{-1}ζ ≡ 1. Defence: the paper mostly uses D^?(χ) as notation. Independent check: Checked p. 84. For v in S with chi unramified at v, D_v(chi) = prod_r (1 - eta^r(varpi_v) q_v^{r-n} chi(varpi_v))^-1 is the inverse of an element of Lambda_{X_p}, and that element is a unit only if 1 - c_r psi([varpi_v]) is nonzero in every residue field. This fails, for example, for r = n-1 when eta^{n-1}(varpi_v) q_v^-1 ≡ 1 mod p. So multiplying by the Euler factors at S gives in general only a pseudo-measure. The reach is wider than 'nothing'. Corollary 9.1.8 is written with the normalized measure (D(chi)·prod_v I_v), and Main Theorem 9.2.2 keeps prod_{v in S} D_v(chi) inside I_S while asserting that L(Eis, phi⊗phi^flat) lies in Lambda_{X_p,R}⊗T. If the measure of Theorem 8.2.2/Corollary 8.2.4 is the unnormalized one (Corollary 8.2.4 does not say which), integrality in those exceptional cases rests on this unproved sentence. v4 p. 82 is the same. Reach: the proof (of Corollary 9.1.8 / Main Theorem 9.2.2 in the exceptional cases).

sourceIssues.locator: Definition 5.3.2, first condition, p. 84, in arXiv v5
sourceIssues.printed: If v is a finite place outside S – so in particular χ_v is unramified for all χ ∈ Y_H^class – then f_v(χ_v,c) is the unramified vector in I_v(χ_{u,v},m) with f_v(χ_v,c)(1) = 1.
sourceIssues.correction: If v is a finite place with v ∤ p and v ∉ S, then …; and one must assume that S contains the primes dividing N_0 (and those ramified in K/K^+), so that χ_v is unramified outside S ∪ {p} for all χ ∈ Y_H^class.
sourceIssues.reason: S is defined as the set of primes at which K_4^p, K_3^p (subgroups of G_i(A_f^p)) are not hyperspecial, so p ∉ S and the condition literally applies to v | p, contradicting the fourth condition and the ramified p-adic sections of §4.3. Moreover characters of X_p = X_{p,N_0} may ramify at primes dividing N_0, where K_4^p may well be hyperspecial; then I_v(χ_{u,v},m) has no unramified vector. The 'so in particular' is therefore an extra hypothesis, which in §4.2 is built into the definition of S (S ⊇ S_ram = S_π ∪ S_χ ∪ S_K). Defence: the intended meaning is clear from §4.2.

sourceIssues.reason: Definition 5.3.2 requires f_σ(χ_σ,c,g) = B(χ_σ,κ_σ) D(κ_σ,m,χ_{u,σ}) J_{m,χ_{u,σ}}(g) with B(χ_σ,κ_σ) ∈ Q̄^× arbitrary, while f^holo of (112) has archimedean components J_{m,χ_{u,σ}} only; hence E_{f(χ,c)} = ∏_σ B(χ_σ,κ_σ) · D(κ,m,χ_u) E^holo, and the 'rewriting' (113) drops the scalar. The mismatch reaches the final formula: I_sigma in Proposition 4.5.6 is computed with f_sigma from (107), which includes B, while Corollary 9.1.8 uses D(kappa,m,chi_0)f^holo, which does not. sourceIssues.locator: §6.1.3, p. 88, lines 12–16 (the characters κ_h^±), in arXiv v5
sourceIssues.printed: The action of h = (h_0,(h_σ)) ∈ H_0(C) on Hom_C(∧^d p_h^±, C) is just multiplication by h_0^{∓d} ∏_{σ∈Σ_K} det(h_σ)^{±2a_σ}; this is just the character κ_h^± = (∓d, (κ^±_{h,σ})), κ^±_{h,σ} = (±2a_σ, …, ±2a_σ).
sourceIssues.correction: h_0^{∓d} ∏_{σ∈Σ_K} det(h_σ)^{±a_σ}, i.e. κ^±_{h,σ} = (±a_σ, …, ±a_σ) (with the paper's sign pattern; the overall sign depends on which of p_h^± is identified with the nilradical of Lie P_0, cf. sourceIssues E90).
sourceIssues.reason: (1) The centre acts trivially on p_h^±. Under (15) (H_0 → G_m × GL(Λ_0^∨), first factor ν), t ∈ R^× ⊂ G(R) maps to (t^2, (t·1_{b_σ})), so the printed character takes the value t^{∓2d}·t^{±2Σ_{σ∈Σ_K} a_σ b_σ} = t^{±2d} ≠ 1, while with a_σ it is t^{∓2d ± 2d} = 1. (2) Direct computation: p_h^± ≅ ⊕_{σ∈Σ} Hom between Λ_{0,σ} (rank a_σ, h acting by h_0 ᵗh_{σc}^{-1}) and Λ^∨_{0,σ} (rank b_σ, h acting by h_σ); the determinant on Hom(Λ_{0,σ}, Λ^∨_{0,σ}) is h_0^{-a_σ b_σ} det(h_σ)^{a_σ} det(h_{σc})^{a_{σc}}, and the product over σ ∈ Σ is h_0^{-d} ∏_{σ∈Σ_K} det(h_σ)^{a_σ}. (3) Modular curve (U(1,1) over imaginary quadratic K, d = 1): the canonical bundle has parallel weight 1 in σ and σc (classical weight 2) and similitude −1, i.e. (−1,(1,1)); the printed formula gives (−1,(2,2)) (weight 4). Defence: κ^D is only used through the intrinsic W_{κ^D} = Hom(∧^d p_h^+, W_{κ^⋆}) in §§6.2–6.5, so the arguments there are unaffected. Independent check: Checked p. 88, with (15) on p. 22, (17) on p. 23 and d = (1/2) sum_{sigma in Sigma_K} a_sigma b_sigma on p. 86. (1) The centre acts trivially on p_h^±. Real scalars t act on Lambda_0^vee by t, with nu(t) = t^2, so under (15) t -> (t^2,(t·1)). The printed character then takes the value t^{∓2d ± 2 sum_{Sigma_K} a_sigma b_sigma} = t^{±2d} ≠ 1; with exponent a_sigma it takes the value 1. (2) Direct computation: h acts on Lambda^vee_{0,sigma} by h_sigma and on Lambda_{0,sigma} by h_0 th_{sigma c}^-1, so the determinant of h on Hom(Lambda_{0,sigma}, Lambda^vee_{0,sigma}) is h_0^{-a_sigma b_sigma} det(h_sigma)^{a_sigma} det(h_{sigma c})^{a_{sigma c}}. The product over the CM type is h_0^-d prod_{Sigma_K} det(h_sigma)^{a_sigma}. So the exponent is ±a_sigma, not ±2a_sigma. The overall sign depends on which of p_h^± is the nilradical (sourceIssues E90). The explicit kappa^D also enters the normalization U^-_{w,j,kappa^D} = |kappa^D'(t_{w,j})|_p U^-_{w,j} in §6.6 (p. 98). Same in v4 and v2. Reach: a stated result (the explicit characters kappa_h^± and kappa^D = kappa* + kappa_h^+).

sourceIssues.locator: §6.1.3, p. 88, 'The identification of G(C) with G_0(C) in 2.6.1 identifies Lie(P_0(C)) with P_h and Lie(H_0(C)) with k_h', versus §2.7.2, p. 28, in arXiv v5
sourceIssues.printed: p. 88: 'identifies Lie(P_0(C)) with P_h' (P_h = p_h^- ⊕ k_h, p. 87); p. 28: 'The identification of G(C) with G_0(C) identifies Lie(P_0(C)) with k ⊕ p^+, and so f corresponds to a holomorphic form if and only if p^- ∗ f = 0.'
sourceIssues.correction: One convention throughout; §6 consistently uses Lie(P_0(C)) ↔ P_h = p_h^- ⊕ k_h (holomorphic = annihilated by p_h^-, holomorphic tangent space p_h^+, Ω^d ↔ Hom(∧^d p_h^+, C)), so the §2.7.2 phrase 'k ⊕ p^+' is the likely slip.
sourceIssues.reason: The two identifications are incompatible. The sign pattern of κ_h^± on p. 88 (∓d on Hom(∧^d p_h^±,C)) matches the §2.7.2 version: with P_0 = Stab(Λ_0) (§2.7.1), the nilradical of Lie P_0 is Hom(Λ_0^∨, Λ_0)^{sym}, whose ∧^d has character (d, (−a_σ)). Independent check: Checked p. 28 ('identifies Lie(P_0(C)) with k ⊕ p^+, and so f corresponds to a holomorphic form if and only if p^- * f = 0') and p. 87-88 (P_h = p_h^- ⊕ k_h; 'identifies Lie(P_0(C)) with P_h'). The two statements contradict each other. By my computation in sourceIssues E89, the nilradical Hom(Lambda_0^vee, Lambda_0) of Lie P_0 (P_0 = Stab(Lambda_0)) has ∧^d-character (d, (-a_sigma)), so the printed sign pattern of kappa_h^± matches the p. 28 convention, as the first reading says. Which of the two statements is the slip is therefore unclear. Either way it is a local inconsistency. v4 p. 25 and p. 87 are the same. Reach: nothing (sign conventions for kappa_h^±; cf. sourceIssues E89).
searched: arXiv:1602.01776 v1 (February 2016), v2, v3 and v4 at the same place: Same in v4: p. 25 (§2.7.2) and p. 87 (§6.1.3).
